bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Sborz shuttled between the bullpen and rotation in three years at Virginia, and he came up huge at the end of his college career. He earned MVP honors at the 2015 College World Series, winning three games and saving another while throwing 13 scoreless innings in relief. After signing him for $722,500 as a supplemental second-rounder, the Dodgers will try to develop him as a starter. The younger brother of Jay Sborz, who pitched in one big league game with the 2010 Tigers, Josh works primarily with two pitches. Neither his 91-95 mph fastball nor his slider is truly overpowering, but they both feature late life that makes them hard for hitters to barrel. He didn't use his changeup much coming out of the bullpen but has exhibited some feel for it in the past. Sborz has an unorthodox arm action that adds to his deception, though scouts don't love it and it hampers his control and command. He has a durable frame and could make it as a starter if he enhances his changeup and locates his pitches more consistently.

scouting_grades_text: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 55 | Overall: 40
bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 55 | Overall: 40 A cousin of former first-round pick and big leaguer Alex Meyer, Hoeing flashed top-three-rounds potential as an Indiana high schooler in 2015 before injuring his elbow and requiring Tommy John surgery. He turned down the Diamondbacks as a 32nd-round pick that summer and the Giants as a 36th-rounder after his redshirt sophomore year at Louisville before signing with the Marlins as a seventh-rounder in 2019. The pandemic pushed his first full pro season back to 2021, when he led the High-A Central in innings (121) and ranked ninth in the Minors in ground-ball rate (56 percent). Hoeing uses his 6-foot-6 frame to create downhill plane on his low-90s sinker, which tops out at 96 mph and is difficult to lift. He also works the bottom of the strike zone with an upper-70s curveball that shows signs of becoming a plus offering. To remain a starter, he'll need to refine his changeup and use it more to combat left-handers. Quite athletic for his size, Hoeing was also a basketball star in high school. He repeats his easy delivery, executes his pitches and commands his fastball extremely well. His 121 innings last year were nearly as many as the 153 he totaled in four years at Louisville, a good first step toward proving he has the durability to make it as a No. 4 or 5 starter.

scouting_grades_text: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 If Brady Aiken had worked out a deadline deal with the Astros in 2014, they also would have landed Marshall with a seven-figure bonus in the 21st round. When Aiken opted not to sign, Houston didn't have enough pool money for Marshall, who headed to Louisiana State but abruptly left in the fall. He surfaced at Chipola College (Fla.) and signed for $750,000 after the Giants took him in the fourth round. For the most part during the spring, Marshall looked like the same pitcher who could have gone in the second round out of high school had he not been strongly committed to LSU. His fastball usually arrives at 90-92 mph, making it an average pitch, but that's OK because he's left-handed, and it might be only his third-best offering. His fading changeup is a legitimate plus pitch and his curveball can be solid at times. Marshall has good feel for pitching and enough control to remain a starter. He lacks projection, so his stuff doesn't figure to get much better, limiting his upside. He'll also have to prove he can stay healthy after having elbow tenderness in each of the last two years, as well as a forearm issue this spring.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Wiseman helped fuel Vanderbilt's College World Series championship in 2014 and runner-up finish in 2015. The best prospect on this year's Commodores after first-rounders Dansby Swanson, Carson Fulmer and Walker Buehler, Wiseman went in the third round and signed for $554,100. While he doesn't have a standout tool, Wiseman contributes a little bit of everything and plays with constant intensity. His best attribute is probably his power, as he tied Swanson and Zander Wiel for the Vanderbilt lead with 15 homers this spring after going homerless in 2014. Wiseman has to let his power come naturally, because his left-handed swing gets long and he struggles to make contact when he aims for the fences. With average speed and a fringy arm, Wiseman probably fits best in left field despite playing right field in college and in his introduction to pro ball. He doesn't always take the most direct routes on flyballs but displays a knack for making dramatic catches.

scouting_grades_text: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 35 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 35 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 45 Wise was one of the most reliable power hitters in college baseball at the College of Charleston, slugging 25 home runs over his three years at the school. He tied for second with six long balls in the 2014 Cape Cod League, and then followed it up last spring with a career-best 12 long balls as a junior. It was that power which netted him a $400,000 signing bonus as a fourth-round selection in the 2015 Draft. Wise had outstanding strength to his frame and generates good backspin from the right side of the plate. He can get pull-happy at times as he did in his pro debut after signing, though there's enough pop in his bat to drive the ball out of the park to all fields. Wise managed the strike zone well in college and should continue to as a pro once he settles in. He projects to hit for a decent average, and especially if he can tighten his approach and trim some of the swing-and-miss from his game. Though he has enough arm strength for third base, Wise probably will need to find a new position as he begins to move through the Minors. He has average arm strength but his throws lack accuracy, while his speed, quickness and hands are all below average for the position.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 70 | Slider: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 After two years as a little-used two-way player at Southeastern Louisiana, Rainey transferred to West Alabama. He went undrafted as a junior first baseman/closer, and was one of the first seniors taken in 2015 when the Reds signed him for more than $400,000 below pick value at the start of Competitive Balance Round B. Rainey ranked among the NCAA Division II leaders in home runs and slugging percentage, but his future is on the mound. He was working at 93-95 mph and reaching 97 with his fastball. His 82-86 slider gives him a second plus pitch at times, though it can get slurvy. Rainey has a physical, durable frame that allows him to maintain his velocity even when he pitches on consecutive days. He has a decent delivery that he repeats well, allowing him to throw strikes. He'll probably be a late-inning reliever in pro ball, though he flashes an average changeup in bullpen sessions and could get a look as a starter, especially given the Reds' penchant for developing college relievers into rotation members.

scouting_grades_text: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 70 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 70 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Duggar was one of the best college athletes available in the 2015 Draft, and a strong Cape Cod League performance had him poised to go in the top two rounds. But he never really lived up to his tools in three years at Clemson, so the Giants were able to grab him in the sixth round and sign him for $248,800. Duggar's best attribute is his plus-plus speed, though he's still learning to get the most out of it. With his wheels, he should be a more prolific and successful basestealer. He also should be capable of playing center field, though he has spent most of his college and pro career in right, where his strong arm is an asset. There's a lot going on with Duggar's left-handed swing, and he can struggle with breaking balls, which holds him back at the plate. He has the bat speed and strength to hit for power, and he drives the ball during batting practice, but he has yet to display much pop in games. Though he has an eye for drawing walks, he gets too passive at times and strikes out too often.

scouting_grades_text: Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 The way his junior season at Maryland started, it looked as if Robinson could be one of those college closers who was drafted early and could make a quick run through the Minors. Command problems forced him out of the ninth-inning role and his Draft stock took a hit, when the Twins rolled the dice in the fifth round. Robinson has the size and stuff to be a legit bullpen prospect, and from the left side to boot. A starter initially in his college career, his fastball definitely picked up a few ticks in shorter stints, sitting in the 94-96 mph range. He backs up the fastball with a slider that can be effective, but isn't consistent. More than anything, Robinson needs to throw strikes. He lost the zone at Maryland then struggled during his brief pro debut. The good news is he's fairly athletic and doesn't appear to have any major delivery flaws that'll affect him from throwing strikes. If he can even have fringy control and command, Robinson should be able to find a role in big league bullpen. Strikes, plus a tighter slider, could lead to his ultimate ceiling of a left-handed setup man.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 A Cubs 20th-round pick in 2012 as a high school catcher, Hickman transitioned from a full-time hitter as an Iowa freshman to a two-way player as a sophomore and a full-time pitcher as a junior. Based on his performance at the Big Ten Conference tournament and the Cape Cod League in 2014, he entered 2015 as a possible first-round pick. He didn't live up those expectations and slid to the White Sox in the seventh round, where he signed for $200,000. Hickman had Tommy John surgery shortly after signing, which explained his velocity loss late in his junior season. When healthy, he's capable of pitching in the mid-90s, but he had dipped as low as 87 mph. His curveball wasn't as sharp as it had been in the past either. Hickman has a big league body at 6-foot-5 and 220 pounds and the makings of two power pitches in his fastball and curve. He also shows some feel for a sinking changeup. Still relatively inexperienced on the mound, he'll need to focus on improving his command once he regains his health.

scouting_grades_text: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 30 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 30 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Finding college bats with power seems tough to do these days, so when a hitter at a good college program not only has it, but shows he can use it in games, teams will take notice. The Mets certainly did, nabbing one of the nation's collegiate home run leaders in 2015 in the fourth round. Thompson's power from the right side of the plate is not in question, with home run pop to all fields, and not just in batting practice displays. He has a solid approach at the plate, though some evaluators have concern about his ability to hit better pitching. The biggest worry, though, is about Thompson's throwing arm, which is well below-average. He's played third and the outfield in the past, and the Mets sent him out at the hot corner, but it seems like first base, where he played this spring, is his best option in the future. Regardless of defensive inadequacies, it's Thompson's bat the Mets bought and it is what will propel him up the ladder.

scouting_grades_text: Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45
bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 There are a good amount of college middle infielders who can hit in this year's Draft class. While Mathias' progress in the field was held up by a labrum injury, he showed this spring that his ability to swing the bat generated plenty of interest. Originally a shortstop, Mathias had to DH for much of 2015 as he recovered from his shoulder issue. His return to the field has come at second base, where he has the chance to be a fair defender. His arm continues to come back, but will likely play no better than average. It will be Mathias' bat that will get him drafted and carry him up an organizational ladder. He has a very good approach at the plate, making consistently hard contact. More of an extra-base hit guy now, there is enough strength for some power in the future. As he's gotten bigger and stronger, he's slowed down to an average runner. College bats who perform always tend to do well in June, and a team seeing Mathias as an everyday offensive-minded second baseman could take him in the top few rounds.

He has improved at every stop in his career and was at his best in 2018, when he led all Triple-A International League relievers in opponent average (.181) and finished third in strikeout rate (12.1 per nine innings). He missed the first two months of 2019 with a lat strain, made his big league debut in mid-July, then was designated for assignment and traded to the Rangers for a player to be named two weeks later. Gibaut attacks hitters with a mid-90s fastball that has tickled triple digits in the past. He throws a pair of quality secondary pitches in a power slider that can reach 90 mph with late diving action and a changeup that grades as well above-average at its best. His three-pitch mix makes him effective against lefties and righties alike, though his control and command leave something to be desired. Though the Rangers assigned Gibaut to Triple-A immediately after acquiring him, he quickly factored into their big league bullpen and could become a seventh-inning reliever if he can do a better job of locating his pitches.

Though Maese can reach the mid 90s, he doesn't maintain that velocity and often works at 88-92 mph with his fastball. His slider flashes potential as a second plus pitch, but he threw it too much as an amateur and it often devolved into a softer slurve. Maese also was a star quarterback at Ysleta High, and his athleticism and frame bode well for him remaining a starter. In order to stick in the rotation, he'll need to find more consistency with his fastball and slider, develop a changeup and refine his control and command.

He has thrived in pro ball, posting a 2.80 ERA, .193 average against and 5.7 K/BB ratio in three seasons before the Marlins selected him in the Major League phase of the Rule 5 Draft in December. Miami will have to keep him on its active big league roster throughout 2023, or else put him on waivers and offer him back to Cleveland for half of his $100,000 Rule 5 price. Enright's fastball sits at 90-91 mph and peaks at 94, but it comes with elite useful spin and riding action that carries it by bats up in the strike zone. He has a north-south attack plan that pairs his heater with a downer mid-70s curveball, creating 40 inches of vertical separation between his two primary offerings. He also can get swings-and-misses with a low-80s slider that has horizontal break, and he'll mix in an occasional low-80s changeup with fade. While Enright doesn't have much margin for error, he rarely makes mistakes, exhibiting plus control and commanding his pitches well within the strike zone. It won't be a stretch for the Marlins to keep him in the Majors in 2023. He has the potential to be one of their more effective relievers.

The right-hander showcased his potential during his pro debut in the Rookie-level Gulf Coast League, posting a 1.66 ERA over nine outings including eight starts, only to have his entire 2016 campaign wiped out by Tommy John surgery in April. When he returned to the mound in July 2017, Fenter showcased much of his pre-surgery stuff during a strong stint back in the GCL. Fenter gets the most out of his stocky frame to produce a plus fastball that reached 95 mph late in the season. The pitch typically sits in the low 90s with sinking action that fuels his ground-ball tendencies. Fenter has good feel for spinning a curveball, giving him a second above-average pitch, and he also mixes in a fringy slider. He threw both sparingly upon returning from surgery, and the same goes for a fading changeup that should continue to get better with greater usage. Fenter has a strong frame and repeats his delivery well, though there is effort to his delivery. The Orioles will carefully manage his workload while continuing to develop him as a starter, though some evaluators believe the right-hander might be a better long-term fit in the bullpen given the strength of his fastball-curveball pairing.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 60 | Run: 30 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Bart turned down the chance to go in the first five rounds of the 2015 Draft as a Georgia high schooler to attend Georgia Tech, where he improved offensively and defensively. The Atlantic Coast Conference player of the year and defensive player of the year in 2018, he went No. 2 overall to the Giants and signed for the largest up-front bonus for a position player ($7,025,000) in Draft history to that point. He continued to impress in his pro debut, finishing third in the short-season Northwest League with 13 homers despite playing just 45 games of a 76-game schedule. Thanks to his bat speed, strength and leverage, Bart rivaled Alec Bohm (No. 3 overall to the Phillies) as the best right-handed power hitter in the 2018 Draft. He learned in college that he has natural power and doesn't have to swing for the fences, and he has the potential to produce 25 homers per season. With his controlled swing and improved plate discipline, he should hit for average to go with his pop. Scouts were divided on Bart's ability to stay behind the plate when he was coming out of high school, but he has put those questions to rest. He lacks speed like most catchers but is relatively athletic for his position, moves well behind the plate and has made himself into a solid receiver. He has a strong arm and threw out 39 percent of basestealers during his debut.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 60 | Overall: 40 A three-year starter at Oregon State, Grenier won the Brooks Wallace Award as collegiate baseball’s best shortstop in 2018, when he helped the Beavers toward a College World Series crown. The Orioles snagged the Las Vegas product with the No. 37 overall pick that June, signed him for $1.8 million and hoped Grenier would adjust to pro pitching enough to keep up with his standout defensive skills. Two seasons in, Grenier’s strong glove, good range, solid arm and strong instincts still make him a plus defender at short. But the bat has been slow to come around, despite the pull side power and solid walk rate he showed in his second run at Class A Delmarva last season. Grenier coupled that, though, with a nearly 30 percent strikeout rate with the Shorebirds, then struck out 34 percent of the time following a promotion to Class A Advanced Frederick. There was some concern Grenier took those struggles with him into the field somewhat, as he uncharacteristically scuffled a bit defensively in 2019 as well. He is also a plus runner who draws praise for the energy he brings to the field. Grenier will always be a glove-first player, but if he can make more contact, he has a chance to fulfill his ceiling as an everyday shortstop in the Majors. If not, he still profiles as a valuable utility-type, someone whose athleticism and solid internal clock allows him to pick it at various points on the diamond. He could benefit from a big year at the plate about as much as any prospect in the Orioles’ system.

Scouting Grades : Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Despite his lack of prototypical size or wow stuff, Moore banked on his track record of success, as a three-year starter at Oregon State as well as during a turn with Team USA, to become a Competitive Balance Round B pick in June. An undersized right-hander, Moore simply knows how to pitch. He fills up the strike zone with a three-pitch mix. His fastball is average, but he can move it around the zone at will. He has a good feel for his changeup, giving him a second Major League average offering. His breaking ball is fringy, with no power to it to be a true out pitch. Moore does get high marks for how much he competes and how smart he is on the mound. While he does have a limited ceiling, his pitchabilty gives him the chance to eventually be a No. 4 or 5 type starter, one who may not take that long to be big league ready.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 There were signability concerns about Sandoval as he finished his high school career in the San Diego area, but the Astros were able to woo the left-hander away from his Southern California commitment by giving him $900,000 in the 11th round of the 2015 Draft. The left-hander made very little progress as a pro until 2018, when he earned a promotion from the Midwest to the Carolina League before being sent to the Angels for catcher Martin Maldonado close to the Trade Deadline, and he finished the year up one more level in Double-A. The Angels might have gotten on the Sandoval train at precisely the right time as he turned in one of the best performances of any left-handed pitching prospect in the game in 2018. While there isn't a true plus pitch in his arsenal, Sandoval does have three above-average offerings and showed tremendous feel for all of them during his breakout. While his fastball averaged at 91 mph, it played up because of its movement and his command of it. The biggest difference maker last year might have been the development of his changeup, which he throws with terrific arm speed and deception, leading to both swings and misses as well as weak contact. His slow, deep curve also flashes plus and he effectively mixes in a slider. Doubters will want to see Sandoval repeat his success. If he does that, he could be a No. 4 type starter and a steal for the Angels organization.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Over the years, Cal State Fullerton has been a veritable factory producing right-handers who really know how to pitch and compete without premium stuff. In 2015, Tom Eshelman went in the second round to the Astros. Two years later, the Phillies took Connor Seabold in the third round. This year, it’s Colton Eastman’s turn and he’s hoping to join his predecessors in the top three rounds. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has been a solid college performer, with a highlight being throwing Fullerton’s fifth no-hittter in history in late March. As a freshman, he was touching 94 mph with his fastball, but hasn’t gotten back there since, typically sitting in the 89-92 mph range. Early this season, Eastman used a plus changeup with tremendous success and showed a below-average breaking ball. Over the course of the spring, his curve has bounced back and flashes above-average, but his changeup has regressed. He’s a strike-thrower, but not quite with the precision Eshelman or Seabold showed during their days anchoring the Titans rotation. Eastman missed a good chunk of his sophomore season with elbow inflammation and has not pitched over the summer in either of the past two years. He’s shown no ill effects this year, though, and a team that believes he could have two above-average secondary offerings to go along with his feel for pitching could snag him early as a back-end starter type who could move quickly.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Thompson became the first player to ever be drafted out of Socastee High (Myrtle Beach, S.C.) when the Mariners selected him the fourth round in 2015. He chose to forego his commitment to Coastal Carolina and signed for $585,000, above slot value for the 125th overall pick, and had a very promising pro debut in the Rookie-level Arizona League. But injuries limited Thompson to just three appearances (one start) in 2016, and the Mariners shipped him off to Tampa Bay in November in a five-player deal. Though he's not overpowering, Thompson has the potential to develop a three-pitch mix of average-or-better offerings. He has a low-90s fastball that can reach 93 mph, and his combination of athleticism and remaining physical projection suggests he'll throw harder and maintain his velocity better with added strength. His secondary pitches lack consistency, but he shows the makings of developing an average slider, and he sells his fading changeup well. Thompson has a quick arm, repeatable delivery and throws strikes, though he needs to fine-tune his command and develop his changeup. After his healthy return to the mound at the end of last season, the right-hander now will try to get back on track with his new organization.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Cutter: 55 | Slider: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 There is no question Minter can get big league hitters out, as he proved during his big league debut in 2017. But given that the Braves' 2015 Competitive Balance Round B pick has more injuries on his resume than accolades, there is reason to be a bit cautious in his evaluation. During his time at Texas A&M, Minter had thoracic outlet syndrome as a freshman, then Tommy John surgery as a junior. He had a successful return to the mound in 2016 as a pro, being used carefully yet pitching his way to Double-A. His 2017 season was also interrupted by injury, a sore elbow and a groin, yet he still managed to reach Atlanta. That's because his stuff is simply that good. He cranks his fastball up to 97-98 mph, his slider has sharp and late break that he can back foot to a right-hander as well as get swings-and-misses or broken-bat contact from a left-handed hitter, and his cutter can be a nasty pitch that hitters can't barrel up, either. He'll miss spots with less than pinpoint command, but he should be around the strike zone enough to be successful. Given his injury history, the Braves understandably proceeded cautiously with Minter and got him to the big leagues at the same time. He has the right bulldog mentality for bullpen work and as long as he can stay healthy, he could be pitching in high-leverage situations late in games for a long time.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Clarke's college career was at a crossroads at Towson in 2013, when the Tigers announced plans to drop baseball and he required Tommy John surgery after hurting his elbow. Though Towson spared its program, Clarke decided to transfer to Charleston, where he became one of the better pitchers in college baseball. He finished the 2015 regular season tied for first in victories (12) and ranked third in strikeouts (126), both school records, enough to interest the D-backs in the third round. Clarke usually deals at 92-96 mph early in his starts and he's able to carry a low-90s fastball into the late innings. His fastball lacks life but still misses bats because his overhand delivery provides deception and downhill plane from his 6-foot-4 frame. His slurvy slider tops out at 81 without much bite and is often fringy at best. He throws a ton of strikes and has a usable changeup, but Clarke's lack of a reliable breaking ball may relegate him to relieving in pro ball.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 A third-round pick out of Maryland as a red-shirt sophomore in 2015, Lowe had a breakout campaign two years later when he established Class A Advanced Charlotte franchise records in slugging percentage (.524) and OPS (.927) en route to Florida State League MVP honors and a promotion to Double-A. When he returned there in 2018, Lowe showed more power and quickly hit his way up to Triple-A Durham, where he homered 14 times in 46 games to earn his first big league callup in August. In the Majors, Lowe overcame an 0-for-19 start to his career to finish with six home runs and a .774 OPS in 129 at-bats. Banking on his future, the Rays and Lowe agreed to a six-year, $24 million extension in March 2019. Lowe has long stood out for his pure hitting ability and on-base skills from the left side of the plate, and he showed in 2018 that he could apply his raw power in games, as he finished the season with 28 home runs and 37 doubles between the Minors and Tampa Bay. He can punish a fastball and produced slightly above-average exit velocities in his first taste of the Majors. He has a good feel for the strike zone, doesn't chase and consistently capitalizes on pitchers' mistakes. Lowe is an average runner but doesn't steal many bases. His average arm plays well at second base, where he's a solid but unspectacular defender, and he held his own at both outfield corners last season even though he was new to both positions. The improved defensive versatility adds even more value to Lowe's bat-first profile and should give him the chance to start on a near everyday basis in the big leagues.

But his stuff regressed as a Draft-eligible sophomore, dropping him to the sixth round in June. He signed for an above-slot $320,000. After touching 96 mph with his fastball the year before, Lakins usually worked at 88-92 during the spring. His heater doesn't feature a lot of life or plane, so he relies on the additional velocity to miss bats. Lakins also got away from using what had been a low-80s slider with nice tilt, but both his curveball and changeup have shown signs of becoming solid or better pitches since he turned pro. He throws strikes but his command is just OK and he lacks classic starter size, so he could end up in the bullpen down the road.

They did add an interesting southpaw a month earlier when they drafted Bergen in the seventh round and signed him for $170,000. Bergen's fastball is more effective than its pure velocity (sitting 88-92 mph, touching 94) and lack of downhill plan would indicate. He has an extreme crossfire delivery that produces nice run and sink and allows him to work inside against right-handers. Bergen's breaking ball fluctuates from a fringy slider in the low 80s to a promising cutter in the upper 80s, and he'd be better off just focusing on the later. He has an effective changeup with some sink and throws strikes, so he could remain a starter and eventually surface at the back of a big league rotation.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 50 | Cutter: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 60 | Overall: 45 The epitome of a crafty left-hander, Duchene has done nothing but win during his college career. He's the No. 1 starter on an Illinois team that closed the regular season with 26 straight victories, and he carried a 22-3 career record into postseason play. He also played a key role in Yarmouth-Dennis' Cape Cod League title last summer, tossing a one-hitter in a decisive semifinal game and winning the championship clincher. Duchene lacks a plus pitch but he might have the best command in college baseball. His go-to offering is his low-80s cutter, and he has two more reliable secondary pitches in his curveball and changeup. He'll vary the speed on his curve from 72-78 mph and fades his change away from right-handers. Duchene's fastball parks around 88 mph and tops out at 91, playing up because it has some running life and he locates it so well. Scouts love his creativity and competitiveness, as well as how easily he repeats his sound mechanics. There are some makeup concerns, however, as off-field issues resulted in a two-week suspension early in the season.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The first time he was eligible for the Draft, Long faltered as a high school senior in 2012 and dropped from a potential third-round choice to the point where he wasn't signable and lasted 39 rounds. He has fared much better in his second chance this spring, following lackluster freshman and sophomore years with an undefeated regular season as a junior at Texas A&M and parlaying that into a third-round selection by the Angels. Long's fastball faded a little bit toward the end of the spring, but he's capable of pitching at 89-91 mph and reaching 93. His heater appears quicker because he unleashes it with an easy delivery, and its riding life helps it play up further. He does a nice job of maintaining his arm speed on his changeup, giving him a second solid pitch. Long's low-80s slider can rate as average, though it gets slurvy at times. He's built for durability but his lack of a true plus offering limits his ceiling to a back-of-the-rotation role. He'll need to refine his control and command to be effective as a starter in pro ball.

He turned down the Diamondbacks as a 28th-rounder to attend college, then went in the 13th round in June and landed a $500,000 bonus. Schrock has bat speed, fine hand-eye coordination and controls the strike zone extremely well, so he should hit for average. Though he's just 5-foot-9, he has some surprising power to his pull side. A stress fracture in his back as a sophomore and injuries to his left Achilles tendon and right wrist kept his numbers down with the Gamecocks, but he could develop into a 12-15 home run threat as a pro. Most of Schrock's value comes from his bat. He's an adequate but sometimes erratic defender at second base, and his average speed and substandard arm make left field his only fallback position. He has good baserunning instincts but won't steal many bases.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Splitter: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Mark was a pop-up Draft prospect in 2015 as a closer at Concordia who set the NAIA single-season saves record. The D-backs took him in the sixth round of that June's Draft and decided to try to let him develop as a starter. He didn't take to it as much as hoped, so now he's back in the bullpen. While he is a bit of an undersized right-hander, his clean delivery and potential for a three-pitch mix made the organization think Mark could work out of a rotation. His stuff backed up in the role, but the year spent trying it out will certainly make him a better pitcher. In shorter stints, his fastball touched 94-95 mph consistently, and he complemented it with a slider that flashed plus at times when he landed it for strikes. He incorporates a good splitter as well, and while he doesn't have pinpoint command, he throws more than enough strikes, especially coming out of the bullpen. After throwing over 100 innings in his year as a starter, Mark has a better feel for his pitches and understanding of his delivery. His stuff isn't strong enough to close like he did in college, but he could have a future as a setup man.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 In three years at Florida Atlantic, Sanger has done nothing but hit, leading the team in batting average three years in a row. His ability to swing the bat should help him in a year where college bats are hard to come by. Sanger saved the best for his junior year, hitting .377 during the regular season and earning Conference USA Player of the Year honors in the process. While he doesn't have the most traditional setup at the plate, he has good timing and a knack for getting the barrel to the ball. He works counts well and has more walks than strikeouts in his college career. He's a little bit of a tweener defensively, without the power for right field or the speed to play center. Even if Sanger profiles more as a fourth outfielder than anything else, his ability at the plate will likely get him off the board in the top five rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Thought to be the best high school player in the state of Arizona heading into the 2015 season, the toolsy Perkins hasn't disappointed, with the outfielder having a solid senior campaign to put him in top five round consideration. A right-handed hitting center fielder, Perkins is a lean, wiry and athletic athlete with raw tools and room to add strength. He has some bat speed and strike zone knowledge, with that added strength, along with better positioning of his hands, allowing him to be a more dangerous hitter in the future. There could be some power there to come as well. Perkins is a plus runner who likes to runs the bases well and covers a lot of ground in the outfield, one who can stick in center field with an average arm. There is some upside with Perkins and the team that believes in that ceiling will take him and try to sign him away from his Arizona State commitment.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Waddell looked like the prototypical pitchability college lefty after two strong seasons at the University of Virginia, including a starring role in the College World Series. He backed that up by pitching most of his first full season of pro ball in Double-A after the Pirates took him in the fifth round of the 2015 Draft. A combination of so-so performance and injuries have caused him to stall a bit. Waddell does have a good feel to pitch and knows how to move the ball around the zone. But he tends to nibble too much and work off the plate, leading to a much higher walk rate than is desirable from a finesse lefty. He has average stuff across the board, with a fastball that sits around 90-91 mph and works best when he keeps it down in the zone to get groundball outs, an average slider and a changeup that usually has good fade to it. The Pirates have preached to him about being more efficient and force contact earlier in counts because he is not overly physical and long innings will make it harder for him to hold up as a starter. He did have two disabled list stints with a forearm strain in 2017. Waddell made up for some lost innings and pitched largely in relief in the Arizona Fall League, throwing better during that limited stretch. He doesn't really have the stuff to be pitch out of the pen, so he'll have to make strides in attacking hitters to reach his potential as a back-end starter.

bio_text: A two-way player during his three years at the University of Michigan, Cronenworth made a steady climb through Tampa Bay's system before breaking out in 2019 at Triple-A, where he showcased some newfound power to go along with an improved feel to hit. He also opened eyes in his return to the mound, despite having not pitched competitively in four years. The Rays rewarded Cronenworth with a 40-man roster spot after the season, then packaged him with Tommy Pham to San Diego in December to acquire Hunter Renfroe and Xavier Edwards. Cronenworth is a pure hitter who has long been able to hit for average thanks to a clean, fluid stroke from the left side of the plate. His over-the-fence power finally emerged in 2019 after he tacked on muscle and adopted a more aggressive approach, and he's always had the ability to manage the strike zone well while getting on base at a high clip. Cronenworth's athleticism and quickness give him solid range at shortstop, where he's viewed as an average defender with good hands who's capable of making all the necessary plays. Cronenworth's biggest asset as a shortstop is the plus arm strength that prompted the Rays to give him another shot at pitching. Serving as an "opener" at Triple-A Durham, Cronenworth operated with a 94-96 mph fastball that he paired with a knee-buckling curveball and a cutter that touches 90. With the potential to offer real value as both an infielder and a reliever, Cronenworth appears poised to become a legitimate two-way talent at the highest level.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The Pirates took college infielders with two of their first three picks in the 2015 Draft. The first was Kevin Newman, taken in the first round out of Arizona. The second was Kramer, selected in the second round out of UCLA. A broken hand interrupted a strong '17 season and Kramer's power started showing up in '18, leading to him joining Newman in the big leagues for the first time. For the first two years of his pro career, Kramer used a contact-oriented approach to rise up to the upper levels of the system. He started tapping into his extra-base thump in 2017 before he got hurt and leveraged his swing more to clear more fences in '18. With that came more strikeouts, but that's not something the Pirates see as a huge red flag. Kramer does need to work on his game plan more, as he does tend to guess at the plate too much. While he's played all three infield positions, he'll continue to see most of his playing time at second base, though he's fine at third with an arm that's bounced back to average. While still in the Minors, he'd have to play second over the hot corner in deference to the other top pick from 2015, Ke'Bryan Hayes, who was the high schooler taken between Newman and Kramer. All three could impact the big league infield in '19 and beyond.

The left-hander missed the 2014 season because of Tommy John surgery, and while he still was not all the way back, he was showing encouraging signs back on the mound in 2015. Before his elbow injury, Irvin threw his fastball in the 90-92 mph range with excellent movement. This spring his velocity was down a tick, but he was slowly getting it back as the year went on. His breaking ball can be slurvy at times, but he adds and subtracts from it with success. He has a good feel for a sinking changeup as well and his command has been solid post-surgery. He's still building his stamina back up, but considering he didn't start throwing until January, seems to be headed in the right direction. With a good pitcher's frame and advanced pitchabilty when healthy, Irvin has the potential to be a mid-to-back of the rotation starter in the future.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 70 | Arm: 45 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 Greenfield School (Wilson, N.C.) had never produced a player selected in the Draft, but in 2015, the Knights had two. White and Dwanya Sutton played together in Greenfield's outfield. White's speed and athleticism made him a better prospect than Sutton, and he was taken in the third round and signed by the Marlins, while Sutton went in the 26th round to the Reds but opted to go on to East Carolina. White is a well-above-average runner who can steal bases and run down fly balls from gap to gap as a center fielder. He has a quick bat and deceptive strength, and while he won't be a big home run threat, he has more pop than the typical speedster. White is extremely raw and has faced little semblance of pro competition, so he will need time to develop. He'll need to develop plate discipline and learn to recognize pitches better.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Depending on when you saw Cleavinger, Oregon's left-handed closer, you saw a potential late-inning reliever with a power arm or a southpaw with poor command and less than explosive stuff who looked more like a specialist. At his best, Cleavinger has a plus fastball from the left side, one that will touch 96 mph on occasion. He'll more typically sit in the 89-92 mph range, leaving some wondering if he has the capacity to hit the mid-90s with more consistency in the pro game. His curve is fringy at times, better when he stays on top of it. He has a quick arm and his delivery does add some deception. The effort in that delivery does make it a bit more difficult for him to find the strike zone more consistently. A team that feels it can unlock that plus velocity out of Cleavinger is likely to take him in the earlier rounds, thinking a lefty setup man might evolve. At worst, Cleavinger does have the deception to be a specialist down the line.

Heinrich's offensive profile fits best in right field and he does throw enough to be able to stay there. He's not overly athletic, but he's far from a sloth on the bases and in the outfield. Heinrich showed he can perform well against good competition. He'll now get to work with the Orioles on proving he can do it on a consistent basis.

He usually deals at 92-95 mph, tickles the upper 90s and has peaked at 99. Smith's fastball lacks life and command, however, so it gets hit more than its velocity suggests it should. As a result, the Patriots have used him mostly as a set-up man, which is also his likely ceiling as a pro. Smith's second pitch is a hard curveball with 11-to-5 break. He's not especially tall, so he needs to stay on top of his pitches with his overhand delivery to achieve some downhill plane. Otherwise, his stuff becomes vulnerable when he leaves it up in the strike zone.

He rediscovered his power at Yavapai (Ariz.) JC in 2015, leading all juco players with 31 homers before signing with the Dodgers as a fourth-round pick. Calhoun continued to hit in pro ball, batting .316/.390/.519 with 11 homers in 73 games while reaching high Class A. His best tool is his left-handed power, which he generates with considerable bat speed. He's not an all-or-nothing slugger, as he does a good job of controlling the strike zone and keeping his swing from getting too long. Where Calhoun winds up playing remains in question. After playing the outfield and seeing some time at third base at Yavapai, he spent his pro debut at second base. While that would be the best-case scenario, he lacks the quickness for second base and probably fits best in left field.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 45 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 A left-handed-hitting infielder from eastern Pennsylvania, Blankenhorn had a very good summer on the showcase circuit, playing well at both the East Coast Pro Showcase in Syracuse and the Metropolitan Baseball Classic held at Citi Field in New York. That performance didn't carry over at first to this spring, but he started coming on strong as the spring wore on. Strong and athletic, Blankenhorn has a solid left-handed swing and a good approach at the plate. There is some raw power to tap into from his frame, though he'll have to make sure he doesn't get too stiff and muscle-bound. A shortstop in high school, he'll likely move to an infield corner, where his above-average arm and solid hands should play well. Whether Blankenhorn can profile as an everyday corner infielder remains to be seen, but those who see his plus makeup and work ethic won't want to count him out.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 35 | Run: 70 | Arm: 45 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 Reds first-round pick Tyler Stephenson wasn't the only blue-chip prospect at Kennesaw Mountain High (Kennesaw, Ga.) this spring. Pruitt actually entered the year with a higher profile and dropped to the 24th round only because he was strongly committed to Vanderbilt. The Blue Jays managed to lure him away from the Commodores with a $500,000 bonus. Pruitt is a true speedster who can cover 60 yards in less than 6.5 seconds and get from the right side of the plate to first base in 3.6 seconds on a drag bunt. He projects a basestealing threat and a quality defender in center field. Some area scouts thought that Pruitt will need to make adjustments to his right-handed swing in pro ball. He has a choppy stroke with some arm bar, and it can get long when he gets overly aggressive. He does have impressive hand-eye coordination and bat speed, so he could hit for average with some power once he refines his swing and gets stronger.

A very strong showing in the Cape Cod League had many interested in the big left-hander, though he hasn't been quite as effective this spring. At his best, Jacome shows strong pitchability without big stuff. He'll pitch with an average fastball, at best, though some hope that his 6-foot-6 frame can handle some added strength which will lead to a few more ticks on the radar gun. His slider works and he has a decent feel for his changeup. He knows how to mix his pitches and move the ball in and out to keep hitters off-balance. Most agree that for Jacome to start, he's going to have to show improved stuff. But his feel for pitching, along with his angle and deception, could serve him well should he end up in the bullpen.

The right-hander gave his Draft stock one final boost by throwing a complete game in the NCAA tournament, and the A's made him their sixth-round pick last June. He signed for $200,000 and then pitched well in his pro debut, only to be traded to Milwaukee along with catcher Jacob Nottingham in the Khris Davis deal. Though undersized, Derby is athletic with a strong, loose arm. He works comfortably at 90-92 mph and touches 94 with his fastball, throwing it down in the zone with significant arm-side run. He throws a tight slider that has depth and late bite as well as a decent changeup, and his changeup has the makings of an above-average pitch. Derby does a good job throwing strikes with his full arsenal, though he could be more aggressive when he's ahead in the count. While many scouts believe Derby will end up in the bullpen due to his size, the right-hander's deep arsenal and underrated polish do give him upside as a starter.

bio_text: 2019 Scouting grades: Hit: 65 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 60 | Overall: 55 The Pacific-12 Conference player of the year as a sophomore in 2017, Madrigal saw his chances of repeating end when he broke his left wrist early in his junior season. He still lived up to his reputation as the best player and hitter in college baseball and became the second-highest-drafted second baseman ever when the White Sox picked him at No. 4 overall (two spots lower than the Brewers took Rickie Weeks in 2003). After helping Oregon State win the College World Series, he signed for $6,411,400 and batted .303 in his pro debut while advancing to Class A Advanced. Madrigal's introduction to pro ball reinforced why scouts considered him the best pure hitter in the 2018 Draft. Unfazed by advanced competition, he used his controlled right-handed swing to spray line drives all over the field while striking out just five times in 173 plate appearances. He's small and doesn't have a lot of raw strength, but his ability to barrel the ball and his plus speed should produce a healthy amount of doubles and maybe 12-15 homers per season. Recruited by Oregon State as a shortstop, Madrigal wound up playing second base for the Beavers in deference to Cadyn Grenier, an Orioles supplemental first-rounder who was rated as the best college defender in the 2018 Draft. Madrigal has the hands and actions to play shortstop, though his average arm makes him a better fit at second base. Chicago planned on trying him at short but he has spent almost all of his pro career at second, where he could develop into a Gold Glover.

bio_text: The younger brother of former big leaguer Nick Kingham, who is now playing in Korea, Nolan spent three years pitching at the University of Texas, the last two in the Longhorns’ rotation, which led to the Braves taking him in the 12th round of the 2018 Draft. He pitched across three levels in his first full season of pro ball in 2019 and after a hot start to his 2021 season in Double-A, he earned his first promotion to Triple-A. Kingham has risen up the ranks thanks to average-at-best stuff and the ability to throw a lot of strikes. His fastball is fringy, at best, averaging around 88 mph. His upper-70s slider and low-80s changeup are both average offerings and he can miss some bats with both of them. He’s not a real big strikeout guy, relying more on getting ground-ball outs. While his stuff doesn’t jump off the page, he commands all of his pitches extremely well. Because he doesn’t have a real out pitch, his ceiling is somewhat limited. His feel for pitching has allowed him to advance and he’s just about ready to help a big league team out as a back-end starter or multiple-inning reliever.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 The top-rated 2016 Draft prospect by MLBPipeline.com, Groome lasted until the Red Sox took him at No. 12 because of concerns about his asking price and his maturity. The Padres reportedly promised Groome a $5 million bonus if he got to them toward the end of the first round, but Boston was able to sign him for $3.65 million, a club Draft record for a pitcher. Groome has all of the physical ingredients to become an ace. He pitches at 90-94 mph with armside run on his fastball and can reach back for 97, with the promise of more velocity as he gets stronger. He has power and depth on his curveball, which is at least a plus offering and might have been the best breaking ball in the Draft. Though he had little need for a changeup in high school, Groome has feel for and some promising sink on the pitch. His 6-foot-6 frame is built for durability, and his athleticism enables him to repeat his clean mechanics and fill the strike zone. If his makeup issues don't hold him back, he has the talent to become the best pitcher drafted and developed by the Red Sox since Roger Clemens.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 70 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 60 | Control: 45 | Overall: 55 Pint had the highest ceiling in the 2016 Draft, so the Rockies were delighted to get him with the No. 4 overall choice. Signed for $4.8 million, he's the best mound prospect to come out of Kansas since Mike Pelfrey contended for the top pick in 2005 and the state's first prep pitcher selected in the first round since Brian Holman in 1983. Gatorade's Kansas Player of the Year as a junior and senior, he led St. Thomas Aquinas High (Overland Park) to the Kansas state 5-A championship in 2016, striking out 12 in a quarterfinal victory and hitting the game-winning two-run double in the title game. After adding 15 pounds of muscle before his senior season, Pint consistently works at 93-97 mph and tops out at 102 with his fastball. His power curveball already is a plus pitch, and he can manipulate it into a harder slider when desired. Though he didn't need a changeup against Kansas high school competition, his already grades as a plus pitch with good fade. For all his upside, Pint does come with risk as well. He doesn't throw strikes on a consistent basis because he has trouble repeating his mechanics and arm slot. The effort in his delivery leads to some concerns about his future command and health.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 60 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 Lewis may have boosted his stock more in the past year than any college prospect for the 2016 Draft. Undrafted out of a Georgia high school in 2013, he played sparingly as a freshman before nearly winning the Southern Conference Triple Crown and then starring in the Cape Cod League in 2015. He repeated as SoCon player of the year in 2016 while contending for the NCAA Division I lead in batting and home runs, making it a virtual lock that he'll become the first first-rounder ever from Mercer. With his leverage and bat speed, Lewis has easy pop to all fields. His swing is busier than most scouts would like, but his approach is generally sound and he tied for the D-I lead with 66 walks entering NCAA tournament play. Lewis is a fringy runner out of the batter's box, but he has solid speed once he gets going. Some evaluators think he has a chance to stay in center field, but most believe he's destined for right field, where he could develop into a serious home run threat with average or better tools across the board.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 70 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 55 Heading into the 2016 season, the belief was that Puk would use his frontline rotation stuff and separate himself from the rest of the class, making him the slam-dunk choice for being taken 1-1. Inconsistency, which has plagued him for much of his career at Florida, not to mention some time on the shelf with back spasms, made Puk more of a wild card than hoped. He ultimately fell to the A's with the seventh overall pick and signed for $4,069,200, the recommended value for the slot. Big and strong, Puk arguably has the best raw stuff of any arm in the 2016 class, with the chance to have three plus pitches. He's capable of touching 96-97 mph with his fastball regularly. Ironically, he might have been at his best in the one inning he threw before his back acted up, showing a 96-99 mph fastball and a plus slider at 88-90 mph. He can maintain his velocity deep into starts and while his changeup is his third pitch, it should be Major League average in the future. Puk's biggest stumbling block has been his control and command, something that kept him from dominating college competition consistently during his Gators career. But that should improve with his ongoing development, giving Puk the chance to become a rotation stalwart in the big leagues for years to come.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Hit: 60 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 60 | Overall: 55 A strong performance on the summer showcase circuit last summer put Moniak on the first-round radar. When he kept raking during the spring, adding some power, he moved way up boards and eventually landed in the top spot of the Draft. The Phillies signed him for $6.1 million, nearly $3 million under pick value, allowing them to aggressively go after talent later in the Draft. While he saved the Phillies money, he had played himself into a legitimate No. 1-pick kind of player. It's Moniak's hit tool and his ability to stay in center field that really stand out. He makes consistent hard contact against good competition. He has a good approach at the plate, spraying line drives to all fields. It's more doubles power now, but he started to show the ability to drive the ball more this spring and should have more pop as he adds strength to his frame. His above-average speed works on both sides of the ball, and some see a future Gold Glove-caliber center fielder. Moniak gets high marks for his baseball instincts and effort, showing an ability to slow the game down as the competition improves. That should bode well for him at the next level, and he's the type who won't let No. 1 pick expectations weigh him down.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 55 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Ray ranked as the Draft's top position prospect entering 2016 because he offered the best combination of hitting and athletic ability. A 33rd-round pick by the Mariners as an Illinois high schooler in 2013, he broke out as a sophomore and continued to star during the summer, leading the U.S. collegiate national team in OPS (.971), extra-base hits (nine) and steals (11). He built on that performance as a junior by hitting .310/.388/.545, with 15 homers and 44 steals. In June, he became the highest pick in Louisville history when the Brewers selected him with the No. 5 overall pick. Ray signed for $4,125,000, just under slot value, and was assigned to Class A Advanced Brevard County for his pro debut. In October, Ray underwent surgery to repair a torn meniscus in his left knee. Ray has a quick left-handed bat and makes consistent hard contact, giving him the potential to hit for both power and average. He uses the entire field well and did a better job of managing the strike zone and making consistent contact this spring. Ray has plus speed and knows how to use it well on the bases, and no player from this year's Draft can match his combination of power and speed. Though he has spent most of his career at Louisville in right field, Ray runs well enough to play center and should get a chance to play there in pro ball, though some scouts question his instincts. He has the offensive production and arm to profile at all three outfield positions, and obviously he'd offer the most value if he can play in the middle.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 55 Senzel was thought to be the best pure college hitter in the 2016 Draft class following a strong Cape Cod League performance last summer and a big junior season at Tennessee, when he led the Southeastern Conference with 25 doubles and finished second with a 1.051 OPS. The Reds liked what they saw and took the third baseman with the No. 2 overall pick in the Draft, signing him for $6.2 million, more than $1.5 million below pick value, but still the top bonus handed out in this class. Senzel combines strength and bat speed from the right side of the plate. He has a patient approach and uses all fields, which should allow him to hit for both average and power as a professional. A solid average runner, Senzel has the instincts to steal a few bases as well. There were questions about his future defensive home, but Senzel worked hard to turn himself into a solid third baseman with a strong arm, good hands and quick feet. Already in full-season ball during his summer debut, Senzel could be on the fast track to Cincinnati. It would surprise no one if he's the first hitter from this Draft class to reach the big leagues, profiling as a solid everyday third baseman at that level.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 55 | Run: 55 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 The most productive hitter on the U.S. national team that won a gold medal at the 18-and-under World Cup in Japan last September, Rutherford began 2016 as the top-rated high school position player in the Draft. Eventually passed by fellow California outfielder Mickey Moniak, who became the No. 1 overall pick of the Phillies, Rutherford still was held in high regard. The Yankees took him with the 18th selection and paid him a well-over-slot bonus of $3,282,000, a club record for a position player. Rutherford has everything he needs to hit for significant average and power. He has a smooth left-handed swing, bat speed and power, though he won't fully tap into his raw pop until he adds some more loft to his stroke. He recognizes pitches well, shows signs of promising plate discipline and generally uses the entire field. Presently a solid runner who broke into pro ball as a center fielder, Rutherford could lose a step as he matures physically and wind up on an outfield corner. His arm draws average to solid grades from evaluators, so right field could be his ultimate destination. Some scouts liken him to a more athletic version of David Justice, who won a World Series ring with the 2000 Yankees.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 60 | Overall: 50 Perez was headlining a strong class from Puerto Rico in the 2016 Draft, when news of a positive test for performance-enhancing drugs put a huge question mark next to the toolsy shortstop's name. The Cardinals rolled the dice with the first of their three first-round picks, signing him for full pick value at No. 23 overall. The first Puerto Rican to be taken in the first round since Carlos Correa and Jose Berrios in 2012, Perez has everything needed to stay at shortstop long-term. He has good speed, instincts, range and hands, as well as a plus arm. Able to make the flashy play, perhaps his only flaw defensively is that he can try to do too much on occasion. Perez's bat is behind his glove, but there are tools to work with. He can ambush a fastball early in the count, but his approach at the plate and pitch recognition need to be refined. Perez's speed works offensively, and he could grow into more power as he matures. It's not easy to find premium middle infielders, a big reason why the Cardinals were willing to take a chance, even given the positive drug test. If that was a one-time mistake, Perez could provide the Cardinals with a first-round bargain.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 Alabama's best prep pitching prospect since Kasey Kiker went 12th overall to the Rangers in 2006, Garrett helped Team USA win the 18U World Cup in Japan in September. He has been better than ever this spring, impressing a throng of scouts with a shutout at the National High School Invitational in March en route to posting a 0.53 ERA and with 131 strikeouts in 65 1/3 innings for Florence High. Despite some signability concerns, the Marlins selected Garrett with the seventh overall pick and then lured him away from a Vanderbilt commitment with an above-slot, $4,145,900 bonus. Garrett featured one of the better curveballs among high schoolers in the 2016 Draft class, a 76-80 mph bender with good depth, though he can fall in love with his breaking ball at times. He also throws an 88-94 mph fastball with deceptive angle and some late life. Both pitches figure to add more velocity once Garrett strengthens his athletic frame. Garrett has feel for a changeup that has shown signs of developing into a plus pitch as he has used it more as a senior. With his loose, whippy arm and clean delivery, he shouldn't have trouble remaining a starter in pro ball. Garrett has a ceiling of a No. 2 starter and a relatively high floor for a high school pitcher.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 55 The son of former NBA player Rich Manning, this 6-foot-6 right-hander was rushing up lists as the Draft approached in 2016, becoming the consensus second-best high school right-hander in the class, behind Riley Pint. The Tigers, never ones to shy away from arm strength, took the Northern California product No. 9 overall and signed him for $3,505,800, exact pick value for that slot. Manning is a premium athlete, one who also played basketball in high school and could have played two sports at Loyola Marymount. He uses every inch of his frame to his advantage on the mound. Though he started late because his basketball team made a deep postseason run, Manning was nonetheless up to 96-97 mph with his fastball in early outings his senior year. He combines that with a hard, power curve that has very good bite to it. His changeup will be his third pitch, but he's shown some feel for it and it should be a viable option in the future, especially with pro instruction. Manning's size, athleticism, stuff and projectability give him top-of-the-rotation potential. Now that he's focusing on baseball only, the sky might be the limit.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 50 | Overall: 55 High school pitching was the strength of the 2016 Draft, and if the Astros had their pick of any of the prep arms, they might have taken Whitley -- who was still available when they exercised the 17th overall choice. A sub-6-footer with a mid-70s fastball when he entered Alamo Heights High (San Antonio), he grew to 6-foot-7 and a low-90s fastball by the time he was a sophomore and continued to improve. After impressing on the showcase circuit and with the U.S. national 18-and-under team following his junior season, he dropped 25 pounds and was spectacular as a senior. Signed for $3,148,000, Whitley has a deep arsenal that begins with a 92-97 mph fastball that features cutting action at the lower end of that range and running life at the upper end. He has a power curveball that reaches the low 80s with tight spin and good depth, and he can vary it into a harder slider at times. He has upgraded the quality of his changeup and his trust in the pitch, which drops at the plate and could give him a third plus pitch. For a big teenager, Whitley has good body control and does a fine job of repeating his relatively easy delivery. Scouts liked how he took it upon himself to better his conditioning and firm up his previously soft frame. He's built like Josh Johnson but is more advanced than the 2010 National League ERA leader was at the same stage.

The upstate New York prep standout was taken No. 3 overall, signing for $4 million. That was more than $2.5 million below pick value, allowing the Braves to aggressively go after other high-ceiling talent later in the Draft. Tall and projectable with the ability to add strength, Anderson throws his fastball in the 91-95 mph range with good downhill angle. His breaking ball can be plus at times, getting swings and misses. It has slurve action at this point, but could tighten up and become a true slider in time. Anderson has good feel for an average changeup as well. He's generally around the strike zone and attacks hitters. While Anderson might have been taken No. 3 overall in a money-saving deal, he has a tremendous amount of upside and could eventually develop into a frontline-type starter at the big league level.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 55 | Run: 30 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 55 Collins has a track record of hitting that dates back to starring with the U.S. 16-and-under national team as a high schooler. He would have been an early-round pick in the 2013 Draft had he been signable, but instead turned down the Reds as a 27th-rounder to attend Miami. He led the Hurricanes to consecutive College World Series appearances and ranked first in NCAA Division I in walks (78) and second in on-base percentage (.544) in 2016, then signed with the White Sox for $3,380,600 as the 10th overall pick. One of the best all-around hitters available in the 2016 Draft, Collins stands out most with his left-handed power. He's strong, owns a quick bat and has good loft in his stroke. He's more than just a masher, however, as he's patient and controls the strike zone extremely well, which should help him hit for average and record high on-base percentages. Scouts are mixed on whether Collins will stay behind the plate, though the White Sox fully believe that he will. He looked better as a catcher during his junior season, though his arm and receiving still rate as fringy. His lack of speed will limit him to first base if he can't make it as a backstop, but his bat still would profile well at the less challenging defensive position.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Slider: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 Hudson was dominant for much of his junior season at Mississippi State and at one point was thought to be a potential top 10 pick. A couple of clunkers at the SEC Tournament and in NCAA Regional play hurt his stock, allowing him to be available to the Cardinals at the end of the first round. They were able to sign him for $2 million, a touch over $100,000 above pick value. Hudson brings plenty of arm strength to the table. He can pitch at 93-95 mph and touch 97 with his fastball, throwing it with run and sink. He couples it with a nasty slider/cutter, thrown in the upper-80s and with true slider break. He also has a solid curve and changeup to give him a potential four-pitch mix. The right-hander struggled with command during his first two seasons with the Bulldogs, but threw more strikes as a junior. Some scouts didn't love Hudson's delivery and thought he could be a future reliever. The Cardinals think he has starter potential all the way and his size, stuff and durable frame all should give him every chance to fulfill those expectations.

His arm bounced back during his senior season in the Kansas high school ranks, cementing his future as a pitcher and throwing well enough for the Braves to take him 40th overall and signing for a well-above pick value bonus just north of $3 million. Whilte Wentz's fastball topped out at 90 mph before his dead arm period, a throwing program while he nursed his arm back to health allowed him to operate at 90-95 mph this spring. Tall and projectable, there might be more to come velocity-wise, and his fastball already plays up because it has armside run and his size creates difficult angle. He has a pair of solid secondary pitches in a curveball with depth and a changeup with fade, and he could have three plus offerings when fully developed. Wentz has good body control for a 6-foot-5 high schooler. His arm action is clean and his athleticism allows him to repeat his delivery and throw strikes with ease. He's very competitive and gives the Braves another potential frontline starter from the 2016 Draft class.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 50 The most talented two-way player in the 2016 Draft, Lowe was regarded by some scouts as the best high school arm to come out of Georgia since Zack Wheeler went sixth overall to the Giants in 2009. The state's Gatorade player of the year, he led Pope High (Marietta) to the Georgia 6-A finals. But the Rays liked him more as a hitter, so much so that they selected him with the 13th overall pick in June, and then gave him $2.6 million to forego his commitment to Florida State. The Rays also signed Lowe's older brother Nathan, a first baseman out of Mississippi State, after drafting him in the 13th round. For as good as he is on the mound, it's hard to ignore what Lowe brings to the table as a position player. He can be streaky at the plate but his quick, controlled left-handed swing and the leverage in his long frame produce considerable raw power. He also has plus speed and arm strength, which should translate into solid defense at third base or in center field. As a pitcher, the athletic right-hander exhibited a loose arm and a relatively clean delivery. He operated at 91-93 mph and hit the mid-90s with his fastball, and he also showed the makings of a solid slider as well as some feel for a sinking changeup. The Rays are confident in his abilities as a hitter and a third baseman, though having him get back on the mound offers an intriguing fallback option should that not work out.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 55 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 A strong summer showcase circuit showing put Kirilloff, a product of the Southwest Pennsylvania high school ranks, firmly on the map for the 2016 Draft. He kept on hitting during his senior season in the Pittsburgh area, cementing his place as one of the best high school bats in the class. The Twins took him No. 15 overall and gave him a full pick value bonus of $2,817,100, the highest a Pittsburgh prepster has gone since Neil Walker went in the first round in 2003. While there is a little length to his swing, he's shown the ability to barrel the ball consistently and has considerable raw power. He's more athletic than one would think given his size and played center field for his high school team. While he played some center during his pro debut, he'll likely be a corner outfielder in the future. He moves more than well enough to stay there. He has a strong arm, one that fired 87-90 mph fastballs from the mound. Kirilloff should fit the offensive profile for an everyday corner outfielder, one who could provide power and run production for a big league lineup in the future.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 70 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 45 | Overall: 55 His brother Justus was a first-round pick of the Indians in 2014, and Sheffield looked like he'd go that early the year before until he had Tommy John surgery. The Red Sox made a strong run at him after selecting him in the 13th round, but he turned them down to attend Vanderbilt, where he redshirted in 2014. Sheffield returned last year to play a key swingman role as the Commodores finished second at the College World Series, then he showed the best pure stuff in the Cape Cod League during the summer. Of all the pitching prospects in the 2016 Draft, Sheffield may have the best chance to develop three plus offerings. His fastball can sit at 94-96 mph and reach 98, and he has maintained his velocity in the late innings of his starts. Both Sheffield's hard three-quarters breaking ball (which is more likely to become a slider than a curveball) and his circle changeup can be out pitches at times, helping him challenge for the Southeastern Conference strikeout lead while fashioning a 32-inning streak without allowing an earned run this spring. All that said, Sheffield does come with concerns. His combination of explosive stuff and small stature draws Tom Gordon and Marcus Stroman comparisons, but his size and his medical history lead to concerns about his durability as a starter. So does the effort in Sheffield's delivery, as he often overthrows and has yet to prove he can find the strike zone on a consistent basis.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 55 Jones took to hockey before baseball and showed promise as a center before concussion issues caused him to focus on the diamond. One of the better high school hitters in the 2016 Draft, he dropped to the second round amid signability concerns but landed first-round bonus money ($2.25 million). After a so-so pro debut, he led the short-season New York-Penn League with a .912 OPS in 2017, ranked third in the Class A Midwest League with an .858 mark last year and posted a .910 OPS during the final month in Class A Advanced. Jones has an advanced approach at the plate, patiently working counts and using the entire field. He has a smooth left-handed swing and impressive feel to hit, and he shows the ability to produce high batting averages despite working deep counts that lead to some strikeouts. His bat speed and strength give him promising power potential that could produce 25 or more homers per season, especially if he adds some loft to a stroke that's currently more geared for line drives. Though he's a below-average runner, Jones is a decent athlete and has worked hard to make the transition from amateur shortstop to pro third baseman. He has a strong arm and has improved his footwork, but still needs to increase his range in order to become an average defender at the hot corner. If he can't, his alternatives would be first base or an outfield corner.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 The Friday night starter for the University of Virginia as a sophomore and junior, Jones helped lead the Cavaliers to their first NCAA title in his first year in that role, then followed it up with a strong junior campaign. Seen as a rather safe college performer who was more high floor than high ceiling, he lasted until the end of the second round, where the Cardinals gave him an above-pick value bonus of $1.1 million. Jones features a heavy fastball up to 93-94 mph, sitting more in the 90-92 mph range. It's more about the plus sink than the velocity and the right-hander gets a ton of groundball outs. He'll throw two breaking balls -- a curve he uses to get strike one and a better slider with good, late bite that often serves as his out pitch. He can mix in a solid changeup with good movement. Starting pitchers from Virginia haven't fared well in the pro game, but Jones seems a good bet to reach his ceiling, even if it's not as high as some others. After a heavy workload this spring, he'll be used sparingly this summer, really getting his pro career started in earnest in 2017.
