bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 30 | Arm: 60 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Coming off a summer in which he led the Cape Cod League with 12 homers in just 27 games, Dalbec drew some poor man's Kris Bryant comparisons and entered 2016 as the best college power hitter available in the Draft. He struggled at the plate for much of the spring, however, and made a greater impact on the mound on an Arizona team that finished runner-up at the College World Series. The Red Sox drafted him solely as a position player and signed him for an above-slot $650,000 in the fourth round. Dalbec's exceptional strength, the bat speed and loft in his right-handed swing and his aggressive approach combine to give him huge raw power. How much he'll be able to translate that into game production remains in question because he comes with serious swing-and-miss concerns. He tries to do too much at the plate, selling out for power, and has yet to prove he can handle breaking pitches on a regular basis. Though he's a well below-average runner, Dalbec showed improved range and consistency at third base as a college junior. He may be able to stay at the hot corner and undoubtedly has the arm for the position. He opened the year as the Wildcats' closer and finished it as a starter -- he allowed two earned runs in three CWS starts and led all Division I pitchers with 41 strikeouts in the NCAA tournament -- with a low-90s fastball and an effective slider.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 60 | Arm: 40 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Louisiana State has had five outfielders selected in the top three rounds of the past six Drafts, and Fraley should go in the same territory in June. A semi-regular as a freshman and a left fielder in deference to gifted defender Andrew Stevenson on the Tigers' 2015 College World Series team, he's the center fielder and offensive catalyst on their '16 squad. Fraley is well suited to bat atop a lineup, as he has a patient contact-oriented approach and the plus speed and know-how to steal bases. His flat left-handed swing doesn't yield much power, but his on-base skills rank among the best in college baseball. Fraley has performed well during two summers in the Cape Cod League. Though he hadn't played much center field for LSU before this spring, Fraley's speed and instincts make him at least a solid defender there. His arm strength is below average, but it isn't considered a liability.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 The son of former big leaguer Dante Bichette, and brother of Yankee farmhand Dante Bichette Jr., Bo Bichette clearly has some serious baseball bloodlines. Though he didn't come off the board as early as his brother did back in 2011, when the Yankees took him 51st overall, Bo's impressive bat still got him drafted by Toronto in the second round (No. 66 overall), not to mention an above-slot singing bonus of $1,100,000. Like the others in his family, Bo does things in an unconventional way, but he has had some success against good competition. Over the summer, Bichette showed the ability to square up quality pitching, and his raw power was on display when he won the Under Armour All-American Game Home Run Derby in Chicago. This spring, he was still hitting the long ball but also was getting tied up on mid-range fastballs inside. While he doesn't have the same exact leg kick setup as his father and brother, there are a lot of moving parts to his swing, which concerns some scouts. He does have more bat speed than his brother did coming out of high school. A below-average runner, Bichette may continue to see time at shortstop, but, in the long run, he's probably best suited defensively for second base, or perhaps even left field. Bichette immediately rewarded the Blue Jays by raking during his pro debut in the Gulf Coast League. There will continue to be questions surrounding his unorthodox setup and swing mechanics, but he's well on his way to becoming a productive, offensive-minded player at the highest level.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The 35th overall pick in 2013, Krook agreed to terms on a $1,587,700 bonus with the Marlins before a post-Draft physical raised concerns about his shoulder. Miami withdrew its offer and Krook went to Oregon, where he dominated as a freshman before succumbing to Tommy John surgery. He redshirted in 2015 and was unhittable when he returned this spring, though severe control problems dropped him to the Giants in fourth round. Though Krook can work at 92-94 mph with his fastball, the pitch is more notable for its outstanding life than its plus velocity. He also has a devastating power curveball that can be a double-plus offering at its best, and he also will flash solid sliders and changeups. In terms of stuff, he has everything he needs to become a frontline starter. Pitchers often need time to regain their control and command following reconstructive elbow surgery, and that has been the case with Krook. He has had to dial back on his velocity in order to try to find the strike zone, and he has had trouble maintaining his high three-quarters release point. He does have an easy delivery and San Francisco excels at polishing pitchers, so there's hope for him.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Szynski threw a perfect game as sophomore at Penn High (Mishawaka, Ind.) and then won five playoff games to lead the Kingsmen to the state 4-A title as a junior in 2015. He boosted his stock with a succession of strong performances on the showcase circuit during the summer and fall, and he continued to impress scouts throughout his senior season this spring. Szynski uses a quick arm and strong frame to generate consistent 90-92 mph fastballs and can reach 95. His high-three-quarters delivery enables him to stay on top of his hard curveball, a solid second offering. He also shows some aptitude for throwing a changeup, though it can get too firm at times. Area scouts say that Szynski has a little less arm strength but better secondary pitches than Indiana high school righties Ashe Russell and Nolan Watson, both of whom the Royals selected in the first round a year ago. His control and command are improving, so there's little doubt that he can make it as a starter in pro ball. He's committed to Indiana.

bio_text: Kansas had its best-ever high school pitching crop in 2016, led by Riley Pint (No. 4 overall, Rockies overall), Joey Wentz (supplemental first round, Braves) and Zeferjahn (a top-three-rounds talent who dropped to the Rays in the 37th because of signability). The first University of Kansas pitcher ever to record triple-digit strikeouts in consecutive seasons, he signed for $500,000 as a third-rounder last June. His scouting reports from high school, college and his pro debut read the same: electric arm, scattershot control. On his best days, Zeferjahn can pitch at 93-96 mph and reach 98 with good spin rates and riding life on his fastball, backing it up with a mid-80s slider that can overmatch right-handers. Yet there are others when he sits at 90-93 mph with a fairly straight heater and has trouble staying on top of his breaking ball, which becomes a low-80s slurve. His changeup shows some signs of becoming an average third pitch but lacks consistency as well. Zeferjahn employs a low three-quarters arm slot and often gets under his ball, detracting from the quality and control of his arsenal. He's most successful when he can maintain a more tradition three-quarters angle but has trouble doing so despite his athleticism. He never has provided consistent strikes, which may lead him to a role in the bullpen, where he might have an upper-90s fastball in shorter stints.

bio_text: The third time turned out to be the charm for Linginfelter in the Draft. Initially selected out of the Tennessee high school ranks in the 16th round of the 2016 Draft by the Yankees, the right-hander headed to the University of Tennessee. He was selected a second time, as a Draft-eligible sophomore, by the Nationals in 2018 in Round 19, but came back for his junior year with the Volunteers. He finally signed as a ninth-round pick of the Angels in 2019, though he didn’t get to make his official pro debut in 2021, heading to High-A after not being able to pitch in 2020 because of the pandemic. Linginfelter has a four-pitch mix that could give him the chance to start if he can find the strike zone enough. It starts with a sinking two-seam fastball that he throws consistently in the mid-90s, a pitch that has led to a solid groundball ratio. His 82-85 mph curve has improved tremendously since his college days and is turning into a true put-away pitch that he commands fairly well. He also has a distinct short slider that plays like a cutter when he gets it up into the upper-80s. He does have a changeup that he mixes in, but doesn’t throw it very often. Whether Linginfelter can control his repertoire enough to start remains to be seen. The Angels feel his overall command has improved, though his feel for throwing strikes can falter, leading to an elevated walk rate. The organization will give him every opportunity to develop all four pitches in a rotation, knowing that if and when the time comes, his stuff could tick up in a relief role.

High has spawned four big league position players, most notably Darrin Jackson, but has yet to produce a pitcher. Martinez, who would have been a two-way player had he attended San Diego State, hopes to break through on the mound after signing for $1.15 million as a third-round pick in June. Though he's not extremely physical, Martinez has an 89-92 mph fastball that can reach 95. His heater had the highest recorded spin rate (2685 rpm) at the World Wood Bat Association World Championship in 2015, which results in riding life that makes it tougher to hit. He also has some power to his curveball, which sits in the upper 70s, and will need to work on his changeup after using it sparingly in high school. One of the younger players in the 2016 Draft, Martinez didn't turn 18 until three weeks afterward. His youth, athleticism and aptitude bode well for his future development. He'll need to add strength but he has a clean delivery and shouldn't have any difficulties finding the strike zone.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 The Padres gambled on Lawson’s upside, giving him $1.9 million (more than twice slot value) after selecting him with the 71st overall pick in the 2016 Draft. In his two full Minor League seasons, Lawson has yet to find any measure of consistency, with an ERA hovering around 5. But he's continued to flash promising stuff and a high ceiling. His overall numbers are hardly indicative of his potential, and he showed signs of a breakout last fall. Lawson put together a strong showing in the Arizona Fall League in 2019, posting a 0.82 ERA with 14 strikeouts in 11 innings, only to have his shortened 2020 campaign wiped out by Tommy John surgery. Lawson operates in the mid-90s with a mid-70s curveball that can be a hammer when thrown right. Scouts believe the curve will continue to improve, but he's yet to show great command of the pitch. Lawson also features a promising changeup that quickly has become a third weapon for him. An excellent athlete, Lawson has grown into his muscular 6-foot-4 frame. He's made strides with the consistency of his delivery, too, but he still needs to cut down on his walk totals. Lawson has dealt with a few minor injuries and plenty of inconsistency, and the Padres feel he's only scratching the surface of his potential. Once he harnesses his talents, he could develop into a back-end starter or a dominant bullpen option.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 50 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Part of a stellar U.S. collegiate national team outfield with Louisville's Corey Ray and Florida's Buddy Reed last summer, Banks can't quite match their tools, but he did establish himself as the best pure hitter on the squad. He led Team USA in hitting (.386) and on-base percentage (.491) and projected as a mid-first-round pick. He wasn't the same after having a cyst removed from his lower back last fall, however, and it wasn't until late in his junior campaign that he looked physically comfortable at the plate. The Nationals gave Banks slightly above slot value as a fifth-round pick, hoping that he continues to regain his form in pro ball. At his best, Banks employs a sleek left-handed swing and delivers line drives from gap to gap. He has above-average raw pop and started to become more aggressive and drive the ball more often in 2015. He didn't look as fluid or powerful during a disappointing regular season this year but did help his cause by winning the Southeastern Conference tournament MVP award in late May in front of a bevy of scouts. While Banks showed solid speed and arm strength with Team USA, both tools have elicited fringe-average grades in 2016. He profiled well as a right fielder in the past, though he's likely to see time at both corner outfield positions moving forward.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 The best junior college prospect in the 2016 Draft, Dietz took a huge step forward last spring after adding strength to his already physical frame. The result was a breakout sophomore campaign for the right-hander, who went 12-1 and posted a 1.22 ERA in 13 starts with 117 strikeouts in 103 innings, ranking among the national junior college leaders in wins, ERA and whiffs. In June, Dietz became the second-highest drafted player in John A. Logan (Ill.) CC history when the Orioles selected him in the second round. After topping out at 93-94 mph in 2015, Dietz now consistently works at 91-94 mph with his fastball and has hit 98 in short stints. His slider has gotten harder and sharper as well, showing flashes of becoming a solid pitch. He also has made strides with his changeup, enhancing his chances of remaining a starter. With his 6-foot-6 frame and three-quarters delivery, Dietz creates good angle with his pitches. He has no problem filling the strike zone, though he'll need to improve the command of his fastball and the consistency of his secondary pitches to make it as a big league starter. If he can't, he has promise as a late-inning reliever.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Webb opened his senior season at Owasso (Okla.) High in 2014 with consecutive no-hitters then blew out his elbow in his third start and required Tommy John surgery. He spent 2015 rehabilitating his elbow and turned down the Indians as a 38th-round pick before enrolling at South Carolina. A rare Draft-eligible freshman, he led the Southeastern Conference with 128 strikeouts in 102 innings before going to the Brewers in the third round of the 2016 Draft. Webb's development accelerated in 2018, and the right-hander finished the year with a strong performance at Double-A Biloxi, striking out 10 batters and allowing one hit in his final regular-season start, then firing another six-inning, one-hit gem in the Southern League playoffs. He struggled to build on that progress in 2019, as a combination of control problems and diminished stuff led to a demotion from Biloxi back to Class A Advanced Carolina, and he ultimately landed on the injured list with tightness in the back of his shoulder in June. Webb's power stuff is headlined by a plus fastball-curveball combo. His heater currently sits in the mid-90s with riding life, and there's a chance he adds even more velocity as he continues to distance himself from the surgery. His curveball, meanwhile, is a 12-to-6 hammer that he throws with power in the mid- to upper-70s. Together, the two pitches give Webb the ability to induce ugly swings-and-misses, which he did at a near 15 percent clip in 2018, while averaging 9.5 strikeouts-per-nine. Webb's split-changeup gives him a third above-average-or-better pitch, one that at times can be almost as effective as his curveball. While Webb's dynamic arsenal and room for improvement give him a chance to remain a starter, most scouts project him as a reliever long-term because he doesn't have an athletic delivery, doesn't consistently throw strikes and his command is even more sporadic. He does create deception with his mechanics and does a good job attacking hitters north and south, using an aggressive nature that could work well in a high-leverage bullpen role.

A strong showing on the summer showcase circuit in 2015 and a move to Cocoa (Fla.) High fueled his early-round aspirations, but a so-so senior season and some signability questions dropped him to the White Sox in the sixth round. He gave up a scholarship from Miami to sign for $700,000, roughly 2 1/2 times the assigned pick value. Curbelo profiles as an offensive-minded infielder. Balls jump off his quick right-handed bat and if he translates his raw power into production, he could deliver 30 doubles and 15 homers per season in his prime. He has a mature, quiet approach but some scouts do have some concerns about his tendency to swing and miss. A shortstop as an amateur, Curbelo has fringy to average speed and fits better at second base, where he saw most of his action in his pro debut. He has reliable hands and solid arm strength, so third base would be another potential fit.

bio_text: 2019 Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 Quintana was a solid high school prospect from Nevada who was drafted by the Red Sox in the 11th round back in 2016, but opted to head to the University of Arizona. He's developed into an intriguing corner infielder with pop, one who could follow in the footsteps of similar players from the program like Bobby Dalbec and J.J. Matijevic, who both were taken in the top four rounds of their respective Drafts. Offensively, it's Quintana's raw power that is his carrying tool. It shows up in games in flashes and he has the ability to hit the ball with authority the other way, to right-center field, but he gets pull happy at times. That leads to some swing and miss and streakiness, but if he can stay with his strengths, he could be an average hitter and tap into that power more consistently. A shortstop in high school, Quintana moved over to the hot corner in college and has become a plus defender there. While the one knock against him is his pure foot speed, he has good first-step quickness at third, with confident hands, a plus arm when he needs it and the ability to make plays on the run. Quintana plays with a confidence that scouts like and there's no question he can stay at third long-term. Some small adjustments at the plate could turn him into a very intriguing run-producer at the infield corner spot.

In a year lacking in the catching and college bat departments, Ice boosted Draft stock with a breakout junior campaign, hitting .310/.432/.563 and setting career bests in most offensive categories. Seeking both value and stability after targeting upside in the first two rounds, the Indians took Ice with the No. 72 overall pick and, after signing him for slightly less than pick value, assigned him to the Class A Short Season New York-Penn League. Ice might not have the offensive profile of some of the premier college backstops from the 2016 class, but that doesn't mean he's not without skills at the plate. The switch-hitter displayed a very good feel for hitting during his junior season, hitting for average and some extra-base ability, while walking more than he struck out. Compared to those offensive-minded collegians, though, Ice has a better chance to stick behind the plate. It's nothing fancy, but he has average receiving skills and an average arm that has been effective at times in controlling the running game. The floor might be higher than the ceiling with Ice, but there's a lot to like in a guy who could develop into a solid everyday catcher.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Thompson starred for the U.S. national 15-and-under team as a rising sophomore in August 2013, dominating Cuba to win the gold-medal game at the Pan American championships. He already threw in the low 90s and looked like a potential first-round pick for 2016, but he injured his elbow and had Tommy John surgery as a junior and then pitched just one inning this spring. The Padres made him its first pick on the third day of the Draft, taking him 85th overall and then giving him $1.75 million, more $1 million above pick value, to lure him away from a Texas commitment. Thompson did hold bullpen workouts for scouts before the Draft, during which he looked as athletic and projectable as ever. He generates easy velocity, reaching 94 mph with some arm-side run and the promise of added heat once he fills out his lanky 6-foot-7 frame. He'll need time to develop his secondary pitches but shows the potential for at least a solid curveball and an average changeup. Thompson's athleticism should allow him to throw strikes and his arm works well, giving hope that he'll stay healthy going forward. It's that combination of feel and projection that has the Padres excited about his future.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 35 | Run: 55 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 50 Louisville didn't have a single first-round pick in the first 50 Drafts, but the Dodgers have popped a Cardinal in the first round in each of the last two years. They couldn't sign Kyle Funkhouser in 2015 but locked up Smith this June with the 32nd overall choice and a $1,772,500 bonus. The third of four Atlantic Coast Conference catchers taken with the first 43 selections, he entered the year with a much lower profile than the other three: Zack Collins (first round, White Sox), Matt Thaiss (first round, Angels) and Chris Okey (second round, Reds). Smith is a significantly better athlete than most catchers, with some scouts giving him plus grades for his speed. He has solid arm strength and such a quick transfer that he consistently delivers throws to second base in 1.9 seconds or less. He moves very well behind the plate and is a good receiver who capably handled several pro-caliber pitchers on Louisville's staff. Smith boosted his profile when he did the same to his offensive production, batting .382 with seven homers in the spring after hitting a combined .235 with two homers in his first two college seasons. He uses a compact right-handed stroke that enables him to make contact with ease. He's more of an on-base machine than a power threat, though he has the ability to pull an occasional ball out of the park.

The Mets took him in the third round two years later as a Draft-eligible sophomore, after Cortes had hit 27 home runs with a .378 OBP in two seasons with the Gamecocks, and signed him for a little more than $1 million. Few, if any, scouts, question Cortes' ability to hit. He has an innate knack for barreling the ball up from the left side and a long track record of doing it against quality competition. Cortes is listed at 5-foot-7, but he has above-average raw power and gets to it in games because his barrel control is exceptional. His frame is a bit thick, however, and Cortes has below-average speed. After manning left field in college, Cortes spent his professional debut at second base, showing fringy range but solid hands and instincts, as well as adequate arm strength. The Mets think he can become a passable defender there -- at least good enough so any defensive shortcomings don't detract from his power-over-hit, bat-first profile.

The Reds hope he can follow the path of 2008 second-rounder Brad Hand, currently in the big leagues. Hanson's spring was up-and-down, understandable given the weather constraints in Minnesota. He sat 88-92 mph at times, 91-94 mph in other starts, maxing out at 96 mph. The Gatorade state player of the year has an outstanding curve ball, though he'll have to throw it for strikes more consistently at the pro level. He didn't need a changeup against the high school competition he faced. At 6-foot-6, Hanson has the kind of durable frame that should hold up well under a starting pitcher's load. He'll have to improve his control and command in order to reach that potential.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Like fellow Tulane shortstops Tony Giarratano, Tommy Manzella and Josh Prince, Alemais was a third-round pick, and he hopes to follow their path to the big leagues. One of the better defenders among college shortstops in the 2016 Draft, he signed for $500,000. He stood out more with his glove than his bat in his pro debut, which was expected. Alemais' strong arm and quick feet and hands enable him to make highlight plays at shortstop. He can get too flashy at times but did make strides with his defensive consistency in his first taste of his pro ball. His tools should allow him to play several positions, giving him utility value if he doesn't produce enough offense to claim an everyday job. A former switch-hitter who now bats only right-handed, Alemais focuses on making contact at the plate. He puts balls in play almost too easily because he rarely works walks, and his approach doesn't yield much power, so he fits at the bottom of a lineup. He shows average speed out of the batter's box but is solid underway and has some feel for stealing bases.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Hampson starred on a big league stage as a 10-year-old, winning the Pitch, Hit & Run competition for his age group at the 2005 All-Star Game in Detroit. After signing with the Rockies for $750,000 as a third-round pick in June, he's trying to continue the tradition of Long Beach State shortstops getting to the Majors. The 49ers have produced four big league shortstops since the turn of the millennium: Bobby Crosby, Troy Tulowitzki (a five-time All-Star with Colorado), Danny Espinosa and Matt Duffy. Though he can't approach Tulowitzki's offensive prowess, Hampson has plus speed and smooth infield actions. He covers a lot of ground at shortstop but his arm is no better than average, limiting his ability to make plays from the hole. His instincts and gamer mentality allow him to maximize his tools. Hampson lacks strength yet sometimes gets caught up trying to hit for power. He does make consistent contact from the right side of the plate but needs to do a better job of putting the ball on the ground and utilizing his speed. Though he has the quickness to steal bases, he'll fit toward the bottom of a batting order as a pro.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 A Phoenix area native who stayed home to attend Arizona State, Woodmansee has been the Sun Devils' starting shortstop for two-plus years, with a solid track record to show for it. It's unclear exactly where he profiles, but college position players who perform well for major programs tend to do well come Draft time. There are definitely some Woodmansee supporters in the scouting industry. Tall and lanky, he has shown some ability with the bat. He has some power to left, though the right-handed hitter can get a little pull happy as a result. A fringy runner, at best, he might not have the range to stay at shortstop long-term. If he has to move to third, then the question becomes about if he'll grow into enough power to profile at the infield corner. At worst, Woodmansee could be a valuable utility type with some feel to hit. A team that believes he has the tools to stick as an everyday shortstop might be the one to take him in the first few rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 A tall and projectable left-hander coming from the Missouri high school ranks, Miller wasn’t drafted in 2016 largely because of his commitment to Stanford. He got bigger and stronger in three years in Stanford’s rotation, though some inconsistencies and uncertainty about his future role kept him around until the fourth round. The Phillies signed him for $50,000 under pick value and if his strong pro debut is any indication, it might end up being one of the best deals of the 2019 Draft. There’s never been any question about Miller’s pure stuff, which matches up against any lefty in his Draft class. He has three pitches that all at least flash above-average, an arsenal that points to a future in a rotation. He’ll sit in the low-90s and touch 96-97 mph, something he was doing more consistently as his junior year went on at Stanford. His slider is a nasty out pitch that misses bats and his changeup was very effective, especially against right-handed hitters, during his pro debut. The Phillies are thrilled with how quickly Miller acclimated to the pro game and he showed a better ability to mix speeds than anticipated out of the gate. Command had long been an issue in college because of some delivery flaws, which led many to predict a future in a bullpen. But much of that was cleaned up in his first summer of pro ball, leading to a much better K/BB ratio. He’ll need to show he can do it over the long haul, but the Phillies feel he has every chance to land in a big league rotation.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Western Michigan had not had a player selected in the first three rounds since Ryan Van De Weg (Padres) and Luke Wilcox (Yankees) in 1995. Akin put an end to that drought in 2016, when he parlayed a dominant junior campaign into a second-round selection by the Orioles. Akin obliterated the school strikeout record of former big leaguer Pat Misch, fanning 133 in 109 innings, as he pitched the Broncos to their first Mid-American Conference tournament championship by winning two games in five days to take home MVP honors. Akin, who was one of the hardest-throwing lefty starters in the college ranks, usually pitches at 91-94 mph and peaks at 96 with late life on his fastball. Though he's not a big guy, he maintains his velocity deep into games and generates it without much effort in his delivery. There's some debate as to which is better, his low-80s slider or his tumbling changeup, but both should be at least average offerings. Akin has three pitches and fills the strike zone, so he'll definitely be a starter going forward. He fared well against quality competition in the Cape Cod League last summer, another point in his favor.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 A transfer from Seminole State (Fla.), Hays had a so-so debut campaign for Jacksonville in 2015. But he really put himself on the map in 2016, showing the kind of offensive profile that could fit well in an outfield corner at the next level, and the Orioles made him their third-round pick in June. The right-handed-hitting Floridian uses a short and handsy swing to consistently make the ball jump off his bat. Hays doesn't waste a lot of motion and has shown both the ability to hit for average and power, albeit it in a weaker conference. It might be more gap pop at the next level, although Hays has shown some over-the-fence ability in the past. Defensively, his plus arm also profiles well in right field, where he is a very capable defender. Hays possesses the tools to be an everyday corner outfielder. At worst, he could be a very productive fourth outfielder at the big league level.

His athleticism helped make him a second-team all-Ohio running back as a high school junior and also made him the highest Ohio State position player drafted since the Tigers took Ron Borquin 50th overall in 2006. A second-rounder, Dawson signed for $1,056,800. Dawson can produce tape-measure shots thanks to his considerable bat speed and strength. He has a sound left-handed swing and steadily improved in three years with the Buckeyes, though some scouts wonder if he'll hit for average in pro ball. He has some swing-and-miss issues and struggled against quality pitching with wood bats in the Cape Cod League in the summer of 2015. An average runner out of the batter's box, Dawson is faster on the bases and has some base-stealing acumen. His quickness isn't as effective in the outfield, where he lacks instincts and will be relegated to left field because he has a below-average arm.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Regarded by some as the best prep player from Arizona in the 2016 class, McClanahan impressed early on when there were general managers aplenty going to see amateur games during Spring Training. And while concerns about his signability made him a wild card headed into the Draft, the Brewers took a gamble by selecting McClanahan in the 11th round, and then gave him $1.2 million, second-round money, to forgo his commitment to Arizona State. After scuffling at the outset of his pro career, McClanahan turned the corner during his second tour of the Rookie-level Pioneer League in 2018. The 6-foot-5 left-handed hitter already controls the strike zone well and shows good feel to hit, with knowledge of where the barrel of the bat needs to be. The in-game power he showed during his senior year has returned as he's grown into his large frame, and there should be even more on the way as he continues to add strength. A good athlete who also played football, McClanahan began his career at the hot corner but now sees the bulk of his time at first base, where most evaluators expected him to land. His athleticism serves him well at the position, giving him above-average range and aiding him with his footwork around the bag.

bio_text: A two-sport athlete at UW-Whitewater, Bachar was selected by the Padres with the 144th overall selection in the 2016 Draft. The right-hander was also an accomplished kicker and punter on the Whitewater football team. His athleticism was readily apparent in college, and it’s carried into pro ball, where Bachar progressed to Double-A Amarillo in 2019. Bachar’s delivery is relatively simple with aggressive arm action. He’s a well-built 6-foot-3 with a four-pitch mix, making him an obvious long-term fit as a starter. He threw 132 2/3 innings last season, posting a 3.93 ERA in a season spent mostly in the hitter-friendly Texas League. Bachar’s fastball/slider combo is his bread and butter. His heater sits in the low-to-mid 90s with some carry, and his slider plays nicely off of it. His changeup and curve have promise as well. Bachar has decent control, but he still has some refinement left with his repertoire. His primary asset on the mound might be his smarts and a knack for setting up hitters. If Bachar makes a few strides, he could be a solid piece for the back end of a big league rotation.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting Grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Curveball: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Romero, signed by the Phillies for an above-pick value bonus of $800,000 to kick off the fourth round, helped Yavapai win the Junior College World Series by throwing a complete-game, 15-strikeout gem in the championship game. Now the Phillies are hoping he can follow in the footsteps of Yavapai alumni like Curt Schilling, Kole Calhoun, Kirby Yates and Ken Giles, and make it to the big leagues. Romero will use a solid four-pitch mix to try to get there. He'll throw both a two- and four-seam fastball, with the former sitting in the 89-91 mph range and the latter touching 94-95 mph at times. While his curveball was his best secondary pitch at the start of his spring, his slider and changeup have improved and perhaps surpassed the curve at this point. He is capable of throwing all of his pitches for strikes. Because of his stature -- he is just six-feet tall -- there have been the inevitable concerns about his durability, with some thinking he'll end up in the bullpen. The Phillies should give him the chance to start, with the potential to be a valuable back-half-of-the-rotation starter in the future.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 40 Though the Royals followed up their pitching-heavy 2018 Draft by taking a pair of shortstops -- high schooler Bobby Witt Jr. and Florida’s Brady McConnell -- with their first two picks in ‘19, they then selected college pitchers with six of their next nine picks, including Murdock, a lanky, hard-throwing right-hander, in the seventh round. After being sidelined for most of his sophomore year at Virginia due to Tommy John surgery, Murdock returned to action 10 months later and delivered 14 starts as a Cavaliers junior, flashing electric stuff that he struggled to control. But he showed improvement on that front during his pro debut in the Appalachian League, and then made even greater strides as a standout at Royals fall camp. Listed at 6-foot-8, 190 pounds, Murdock is an imposing presence on the mound who has become significantly stronger since entering the pro ranks. Those physical gains have helped the fast-armed righty add more velocity to a heavy fastball that now touches 99 mph and sits comfortably in the mid 90s. A high-spin curveball gives Murdock a second plus pitch as well as a weapon against righties, and he’s shown improving feel for a power slider that dives across the zone. Club officials are quick to praise Murdock’s promising changeup even though he’s had limited opportunities to deploy it as a pro. The Royals feel that Murdock, with his blend of size, stuff and low-mileage arm, is only scratching the surface of his potential and believe he has enough starter qualities to be developed in that role. But in order to achieve that, Murdock will first need to improve the sync and consistency in his delivery and show that he can hold his stuff deep into his starts. If that doesn’t work out, Murdock’s power stuff could make him a bullpen weapon.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 55 As the 2016 Draft approached, Balazovic traveled to Florida with his fellow Canadian high school standouts. The right-hander separated himself with his performance and projectability and the Twins took him in the fifth round that June, going above slot to sign him away from his Auburn commitment. After two summers in the Gulf Coast League, he took a nice step forward while pitching full-season ball for the first time, then another leap in 2019. Balazovic made very good strides during extended spring training and that carried over into his 2018 Midwest League debut. The big right-hander had plenty left in the tank at the end of the year, living in the 92-94 mph range and consistently up to 95 mph with his fastball, and he's been up to 97 mph consistently this season. He throws it with good sinking action to get ground-ball outs. His changeup has improved quite a bit, and while he can still throw it a bit too hard, in the 85-86 mph range, it has more movement and there's more separation between the two pitches because of his uptick in velocity. The slider is still his go-to breaking ball and it flashes plus. There could still be more in the tank as Balazovic continues to fill out his 6-foot-4 frame, giving him considerable ceiling. He's taken a nice step in the right direction toward reaching it, with a big up arrow next to his name, this season.

bio_text: 2019 Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 60 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After three years pitching out of the University of Alabama bullpen, Burrows left as the school's career leader in saves with 30. Seeing him as a future left-handed big league reliever, the Mariners took him in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft. He spent just one summer with Seattle as he was sent to the Braves in January 2017, along with Luiz Gohara in return for Mallex Smith and Shae Simmons. He reached Double-A in 2018, his second season in the organization, then capped things off in the Arizona Fall League. Burrows' calling card is his breaking ball, and it's a real weapon against left-handed hitters but nasty enough to miss right-handed bats as well. He throws it with deception with late, sharp break, and hitters don't see it. It's the main reason why he carries a 12.2 K/9 ratio into the 2019 season. His fastball sits in the low-90s coming from a low three-quarters slot, allowing it to play up beyond the velocity. Burrows' progress has been slowed a bit by a lack of consistency and command, though it's clear his two-pitch mix is plenty to get big league hitters out. At the very least, he's a left-handed specialist. At the top end, he's a seventh-inning type reliever, with an Eric O'Flaherty career path.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Hill pitched just 18 2/3 innings as a freshman last year and opened 2016 in Texas A&M's bullpen. By early April, he had taken over as the Aggies' No. 1 starter and responded with six quality starts in eight tries. He led the Southeastern Conference with a 1.88 ERA as A&M ranked No. 1 in the nation headed into NCAA tournament play. Hill has maintained the quality of his stuff and shown a third pitch since he moved to the rotation. He sits in the low 90s and can reach 96 mph with his fastball. His low-80s slider is a plus pitch at times, while his changeup can be a bit firm but generally is effective. Though Hill throws strikes with ease and has excelled as a starter, there still are questions about his long-term durability in that role. He's an undersized right-hander who had Tommy John surgery in high school four years ago. He's Draft-eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore, giving him some additional negotiating leverage.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 35 | Run: 50 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Justus started at shortstop for three years at Georgia Tech. For the first two, he was known mostly for his ability with the glove. A big step forward with the bat as a junior allowed him to be thought of as one of the best all-around prospects at the position and landed him in the fifth round, where he signed with the Angels for nearly $100,000 below pick value. While Justus lacks a plus tool, he does have the chance to hit and stay at short, which puts him ahead of many of his college counterparts. He's an average runner with a solid arm and gets the job done at the premium position without any flash, relying on good anticipation and a quick first step. He has fast hands and can make throws from a variety of angles. While he might be a bottom-of-the-order hitter at the highest level, he does make consistent contact and started driving the ball with more authority than he used to during his junior season. He's not a plus runner, but he does have excellent baserunning instincts. Justus may not wow anyone with tools, but he's the kind of solid performer who ends up as an everyday shortstop on a winning Major League roster.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 65 | Arm: 40 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 Wrenn's center-field profile and a strong summer in the Cape Cod League in 2015 positioned him to go in the top three rounds of the 2016 Draft. But a ball tipped off his glove and broke three bones in his face right before his junior season at Georgia, and he didn't hit as well as he had as a sophomore. That allowed the Astros to grab him in the sixth round and sign him for $257,900. Wrenn's best tool is his speed, which some evaluators grade as a 70 on the 20-80 scouting scale. It makes him an obvious basestealing threat, though he doesn't swipe as many bags or succeed on as many attempts as his quickness should allow. His speed gives him plenty of range in center field and his arm is playable there. Though his wheels could translate into on-base ability at the top of a lineup, Wrenn still is seeking his identity at the plate. He displayed some intriguing pull power when he ranked fifth in the Cape with five homers and went deep six times in his first two weeks as a pro. He sometimes gets caught in between the two approaches and swings and misses more than he should, though scouts praise his makeup and think he could be better in pro ball than he was in college.

Tyler was a 30th-round pick out of an Illinois high school by the Red Sox in the 2016, sliding because of his commitment to Louisville, and scouts thought he had the chance to emerge as a first-rounder after three years of college. That won't quite happen, though a surge in the month leading up to the Draft could carry him as high as the third round. While Fitzgerald doesn't have loud tools, he's a steady performer in all facets of the game. He has improved offensively throughout his college career, making regular contact to all fields from the right side of the plate. He's not a slugger but he has a strong 6-foot-3 frame and has hit the ball harder this spring, so he could have 12-15 home run power if he continues to develop. Fitzgerald has average to above-average speed and good savvy on the bases. He's not the rangiest shortstop, though he makes plays with his reliable hands and solid, accurate arm. If he can't stick at shortstop, he might not produce enough offense to profile as a regular at second or third base, but he does have a high floor as a utilityman.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After a solid high school career in Alabama, Daniel stepped right into Auburn’s rotation as a freshman, then both started and relieved as a Draft-eligible sophomore when he was taken in the 11th round of the 2018 Draft. He was set to be a part of Auburn’s rotation in 2019 but got shut down after two innings in his first start, undergoing Tommy John surgery in April 2019. The Angels took him in the seventh round of that June’s Draft anyway, signing him for a bit under slot. He didn’t pitch in any capacity for the organization until instructs last fall, where he made a very strong first impression. A 6-foot-1 right-hander, Daniel uses a very efficient and smooth delivery to deliver a solid, if unspectacular, three-pitch mix. His fastball tops out at around 93 mph, but he gets swings and misses on it thanks to high spin rates up in the zone. He complements his fastball with a solid breaking ball and good feel for a changeup. When he was healthy, Daniel did struggle with his command and control, walking 4.3 per nine innings as a sophomore. His repertoire and feel for pitching point to the potential to start, but his fastball did tick up when he pitched out of the pen for Auburn in 2018.

In his first full pro season, he ranked third in the Minors in K/BB ratio (10.1) and walk rate (0.8 per nine innings). He continued to throw four pitches for strikes in 2018, overcoming a lat strain to hold his own in Double-A. Civale's lone plus pitch is a cutter/slider that he throws at 85-88 mph. His four-seam fastball has fringy low-90s velocity but is effective because it has a high spin rate and he commands it exceptionally well. While neither his curveball nor changeup stands out for its quality, he does a nice job of sequencing them with his cutter and fastball. Though he's following Shane Bieber's path and has the best command in the system, it's uncertain whether Civale can start in the Majors. His strikeout rate has declined as he has risen through the Minors, leading to questions as to whether he'll miss enough bats as a big league starter. He could find more success as a multi-inning reliever who focuses on cutters and well-placed fastballs.

Behind the plate, he's a decent receiver with an acceptable arm. Nothing he does jumps out as plus, but he's been doing everything fairly well during his junior season, and doing it that way consistently. While some scouts question his ability to be a big league regular behind the plate, his strong junior campaign has shown that perhaps he can stick there. The team that takes him in the top four rounds will think he has the chance to reach that ceiling.

bio_text: Scouting Grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 After missing the 2014 season at Oregon following Tommy John surgery, Irvin returned in 2015 and worked to shake off the rust. He struggled at the outset of the 2016 season, but it appears a switch went off late in the spring as he took over the Ducks' role as Friday night starter and looked more like the prospect he was coming out of high school. The twice-drafted Irvin is the epitome of the advanced college lefty when he his firing on all cylinders. For much of the time since he returned from surgery, Irvin had been throwing his fastball in the 86-88 mph range, but was up to 93-94 mph consistently late in his redshirt junior season thanks to some added strength. His slider and changeup will flash above-average at times and he does a good job of throwing everything with the same arm speed to add deception. A good athlete with a solid pickoff move, he throws a lot of strikes, though he can be susceptible to the home run ball. Irvin's ceiling is limited to that of a back-end starter, but he is really polished and if he is the guy he was late in the spring, he's a high probability big leaguer.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Shawaryn won 13 games and struck out 138 batters as a sophomore in 2015, setting Maryland school records and leading all NCAA Division I pitchers returning to college in 2016. He had first-round aspirations entering the year but had an up-and-down junior season before finishing with a 16-strikeout complete game in the Big Ten Conference tournament. He fell to the Red Sox in the fifth round but landed an above-slot $637,500 bonus. The Terrapins' career leader in wins (30) and strikeouts (307), Shawaryn works from a low three-quarters slot that adds life to his pitches, all of which have the potential to be at least solid. His fastball usually runs from 90-94 mph with sink, though his velocity was down to 86-88 at times early in the college season. His sweeping slider can get swings and misses from both lefties and righties, and he shows some feel for a fading changeup. Shawaryn has a strong, durable build that lets him maintain his stuff over the course of a game and a season. He fills the strike zone, too, though some scouts wonder if he might be better suited as a reliever because of his arm angle. In shorter stints, he might have two plus offerings with his fastball and slider.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 45 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 The final player (1,216th overall) taken in the 2013 Draft -- more of a reflection of his signability than his ability -- Anderson blossomed into a third-rounder after three years at Florida. Part of a loaded Gators pitching staff that included five arms taken in the first four rounds of the 2016 Draft as well as the potential first college hurlers selected in the 2017 and 2018 Drafts, he recorded 13 saves and a 0.97 ERA as their closer last spring. Signed for $700,000, he looked rusty when he made his pro debut after a six-week layoff, giving up nine runs in two brief outings. Coming out of the Florida bullpen, Anderson pitched at 92-95 mph and hit 96 with some sink and run on his fastball. He also got some swings and misses with a slider/cutter that shows flashes of becoming a plus offering. It has good depth when he throws it in the mid-80s and cut action when he delivers it in the upper 80s. Though he made just one start in three years of college, Anderson is equipped to work out of the rotation in pro ball and could get that opportunity in 2017. He has a deep repertoire that also includes a fading changeup and a decent curveball. He throws a lot of strikes and is at his best when he uses his 6-foot-4 frame to pound the bottom of the strike zone.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 45 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Scouts saw plenty of Abreu when they were scouting Albert Almora (the sixth overall pick in the 2012 Draft) at Mater Academy Charter High (Hialeah Gardens, Fla.), and he had the tools to go in the top five rounds the following year. After he turned down the Reds as a 14th-rounder, he never quite put up big numbers in three years at Miami, though he did help the Hurricanes reach a pair of College World Series. A sixth-round selection in 2016, he hit 14 homers and stole 40 bases in low Class A during his first full pro season. Abreu's bat speed, strength and leverage create well above-average raw power from the left side of the plate, but he's not going to get to use all of it unless he improves as a hitter. He's overly aggressive, which leads to swing-and-misses and a lot of weak contact on pitches he'd be better off avoiding rather than putting in play. Whether he can make adjustments and provide more consistent pop remains to be seen. Abreu moves well for a 6-foot-4, 225-pounder but his 40 steals are as much a product of his instincts than his average speed. He has plus arm strength and showed it off by leading the South Atlantic League with 16 outfield assists in 2017. He gets the job done in right field and could fill in for short periods in center.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Feliciano and shortstop Delvin Perez headlined a strong crop of talent from Puerto Rico in the 2016 Draft. While Perez went to the Cardinals in the first round, Feliciano, an offensive-minded catcher, remained on the board until Lottery Round B, where the Brewers took him with the No. 75 overall pick. The key to unlocking Feliciano's potential lies in is his bat. He has some strength in his swing, with over-the-fence potential, but he's not an all-or-nothing hitter and shows a solid approach at times. Especially for a catcher, Feliciano runs well, and that athleticism translates in his efforts behind the plate. He has a solid arm, though some worry about his overall defensive game and ability to catch long-term. If he can't stay behind the plate, there's a chance Feliciano could handle left field, though that might be a stretch. Regardless of his future defensive home, Feliciano's offensive potential will be his calling card moving forward.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 50 In 2016, the Braves took four high school pitchers with their top six picks and signed all of them. Wilson, a prepster from North Carolina, was the last of the quartet, getting $1.2 million to forgo his commitment to the University of North Carolina. After leading the system in ERA in his first full season, he streaked across three levels of the Minors to make his big league debut in 2018, the first high schooler from his Draft class to do so. Once upon a time, people saw Wilson as a future reliever because of his size, stuff and bulldog mentality. A former high school football player, Wilson goes right after hitters with his three-pitch arsenal. His fastball typically sits in the low-90s, but he's shown the ability to ratchet it up to 97-98 mph at times, and he throws it with a lot of sink to get ground-ball outs. His breaking ball still gets slurvy at times and can look like a slider or a curve depending on when you see it, but it's an effective pitch, especially when it's harder and tighter. His changeup keeps improving and flashes above-average at times. All of his stuff plays up because he can command it well and has shown fearlessness on the mound throughout his quick run up the organizational ladder. He's convinced evaluators he can start, with a ceiling perhaps as a mid-rotation starter, though the Braves' pitching depth could send him to the bullpen, at least in the short-term.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 60 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Hess' electric arm could have made him a top-five-rounds pick out of a Virginia high school in 2016, but his steadfast commitment to Louisiana State dropped him all the way to the Yankees in the 35th round. He opened his freshman season as a midweek starter before becoming a dominating closer in April and playing a key role in the Tigers' runner-up finish at the College World Series. He moved into the weekend rotation this spring to fill a need, and though most scouts still envision him as a reliever, he's talented enough to go in the first three rounds as a Draft-eligible sophomore. As a starter, Hess usually works with a 91-95 mph fastball and a solid slider. When he came out of the bullpen last year, he repeatedly ran his heater into upper 90s and backed it up with a wipeout slider. He uses his low-three-quarters arm slot and 6-foot-6 frame to create angle and life that make both pitches difficult to contend with. Hess has yet to show much aptitude for a changeup, but also hasn't really needed one yet. He has toned down his delivery some but still throws with effort, and his arm action and fringy control may have him ticketed for the bullpen in pro ball. If a pro team makes him a reliever, he could be one of the first players in the 2018 Draft to reach the big leagues.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 55 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 55 Thompson was as talented as any high school left-hander in the Midwest in 2016, which could have landed him in the top five rounds had concerns about his shoulder and his commitment to Kentucky not caused the Indiana prepster to slide to the Rays in the 11th. He still would have landed a well-over-slot bonus from Tampa Bay if he hadn't failed a post-Draft physical. More medical questions arose when he missed two months as a sophomore with an elbow injury that didn't require surgery. He has stayed healthy and done a much better job of throwing strikes in 2019, putting himself in position to be one of the first pitchers drafted. As a southpaw with a strong frame and four pitches, Thompson has the ingredients to become a mid-rotation starter. Both his fastball, which sits in the low 90s and tops out at 96 mph with some run and angle, and his low-80s slider are plus pitches at their best. He generates good spin rates on both his slider and curveball, which has more depth than power, and also mixes in a decent changeup. Though some clubs still have concerns about Thompson's health history, he has helped his cause by not missing a start and working deeper into games this spring. His high-three-quarters delivery is relatively clean, and he's finally pounding the strike zone after battling it in his first two college seasons. He has a good chance to surpass Alex Meyer (No. 23 overall, 2011) for the distinction of being the highest-drafted pitcher ever from the Wildcats program.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 55 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 50 A second-round pick out of Louisville by the Yankees in 2016, Solak has produced consistently throughout his pro career -- which has made him attractive to other teams. The Rays acquired him from New York as part of a three-team deal in February 2018, sending outfielder Steven Souza to the D-backs and also receiving pitching prospects Anthony Banda, Colin Poche and Sam McWilliams from Arizona. The Rangers picked up Solak this July in exchange for Pete Fairbanks. A pure hitter, Solak makes repeated line-drive contact with a quick right-handed swing and a hit-to-all-fields approach. He manages the strike zone well and consistently puts together good at-bats, employing a selectively aggressive approach that fuels his ability to hit for average and also get on base at a high clip. He has shown more power in the last two seasons and could hit 15 or more annually as an everyday player in the big leagues, and his solid speed and instincts make him a threat to steal. Solak has a below-average arm and isn't the most fluid second baseman, but he has worked hard to improve his footwork at the keystone and makes all the routine plays. The Rays started to increase his versatility last year with reps in the outfield, and Solak has held his own in both left field and center to go along with his usual work on the dirt. Regardless of his future position, it will be Solak's blend of hitting ability and speed that gets him to the big leagues.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 45 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 For his first two years at Louisville, Harrington pitched largely out of the bullpen. The left-hander moved to the rotation as a junior and was named the Atlantic Coast Conference's pitcher of the year. His performance moved him into the third round where the Braves grabbed him. He pitched sparingly in his pro debut after the long college season but is ready to attack pro ball as a starter. Harrington is definitely pitchability and command over pure stuff. He'll throw his fastball in the 86- to 92-mph range. It plays up because of its sink and because he locates it so well at the bottom of the strike zone. He has a decent three-quarters breaking ball and a changeup, both of which can grade out as Major League average. There is a ton of deception to his delivery, and he pounds the zone with quality strikes, keeping hitters from squaring up his pitches. Harrington's stuff does play up a tick if he's coming out of the bullpen, but his command, deception and competitiveness all point to him having a future as a back-of-the-rotation starter. If it doesn't work, he could move very quickly as a middle reliever.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 50 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 One of the best two-way prospects in the 2016 Draft, Lee intrigued several clubs as a left-handed pitcher with a fastball that tops out at 94 mph and a solid slider. Kansas City preferred Gatorade's Virginia player of the year as an outfielder and made him a full-time position player after signing him for $750,000 as a third-round pick. The Royals believed Lee was the best athlete available when they drafted him with the 103rd overall choice, and he has the potential for average or better tools across the board. He has surprising pop for someone 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, the product of quality bat speed from the left side of the plate. He has a line-drive stroke and a patient approach that should help him hit for average. Lee is an average runner out of the batter's box and a little quicker on the bases. He played primarily center field while also manning both corners in his pro debut, and he figures to end up in right field. He could be a solid defender there and definitely has the arm strength required for the position.

Bieber, a three-year starter, continued that trend in 2016 when he signed with Cleveland as its fourth-round pick. Bieber is the epitome of the advanced, yet not exciting, college arm. A Sunday starter a year ago, the right-hander served as UC Santa Barbara's Friday night starter in 2016, after his strong showing in the Cape Cod League last summer. The right-hander lacks a true out pitch but effectively employs three average offerings. He generally pitches around 90-91 mph with his heater, but there could be some more velocity to unlock at the next level. He mixes in a solid slider and changeup and demonstrates exemplary control of all three pitches. A lack of a true out pitch limits Bieber's ceiling, but his polish, durability and track record suggests that he could move quickly.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Cody started the Cape Cod League all-star game in 2014, highlighting a summer in which he positioned himself as a likely first-round candidate for the 2015 Draft. He struggled early that spring before rallying late in the season and going in the second round to the Twins. Negotiations broke down over concerns about his elbow, so he returned to Kentucky for his senior season, during which he started slowly but finished strong once again. Cody's stuff has looked pretty much the same as it did a year ago. He has one of the better fastballs among college starters, working at 92-95 mph and hitting 98. He generates easy velocity with a 6-foot-7, 245-pound frame that also creates difficult angle and plane on his pitches. His slurvy breaking ball has been a little less sharp this spring, though Cody shows a solid low-80s slider when he stays on top of the pitch. He rarely employs his changeup but has shown some decent feel for it in the past. He throws enough strikes and has a ceiling of a workhorse starter, though some scouts think his inconsistent command means he'll have more success as a high-leverage reliever.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Williams first made a name for himself when he struck out 17 batters in a game at the 2007 Little League World Series, and he later starred on a U.S. national team that won a gold medal at the 2012 18-and-under world championships. Projected as a first-round pick in the 2013 Draft out of high school, he had thoracic outlet surgery prior to his senior season and lasted until the Padres took him in 33rd round. He showed first-round stuff in two summers in the Cape Cod League and during fall practice in 2015, but he's now a wild card after pitching just 10 2/3 innings during the regular season. Last fall, Williams showed two well above-average pitches in a 93-96 mph fastball with riding life and a true hammer curveball in the upper 70s. Despite having two swing-and-miss offerings, he rarely has trusted his stuff, which has led to him having difficulty throwing strikes and earning much of a role at Oklahoma State. Neither his fastball nor his curve has been as sharp in limited action in 2016. Williams has flashed a decent changeup in the past and almost certainly will get a chance to start in pro ball, which at least will give him some much-needed innings. Whatever his role, he'll need to do a better job of repeating his lower-three-quarters delivery and commanding his premium stuff. There also are questions about his health after he missed the first five weeks this season with shoulder tendinitis.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After producing just one top-three-rounds pitcher (Scott Schoeneweis) in the first 47 Drafts, Duke has had two in the past four years with Marcus Stroman and Michael Matuella. The Blue Devils had a chance for another in Clark, who starred in brief stints in the Cape Cod League and with the U.S. collegiate national team last summer. He looked like a possible first-rounder when he showed a mid-90s fastball while allowing a total of three runs in his first three starts this spring, but then his velocity and command dipped and he found himself out of the weekend rotation by mid-April. Clark was on scouts' radar when he went undrafted as a North Carolina high schooler in 2013, and his stuff has picked up as he has matured physically in college. His fastball can reach 99 mph and features nasty run and sink when it's at his best, and he has made strides with his 83-86 mph slider that also can be overpowering at times. However, there's a significant amount of effort in his delivery, which makes it tough for him to maintain his velocity and locate his pitches. Evaluators don't love Clark's arm action either, and a growing number believe he's destined for the bullpen in pro ball. He wouldn't have to worry about pacing himself or having to be as fine with his pitches in shorter stints, and he might have closer upside if he improved the consistency of his breaking ball. If he's going to stay in the rotation, he'll need to improve his changeup.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 55 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 40 | Overall: 45 Yerzy, a native of Toronto, really put himself firmly on the map during the High School Select home run derby held over the 2015 All-Star Game weekend in Cincinnati, advancing to the finals and getting to swing with the Major Leaguers in the main event on Monday. Team Canada's annual tour through Florida this spring gave Yerzy the chance to raise his stock, and he took advantage, landing in the second round and getting full pick value -- $1,214,100 -- to sign with the D-backs. Yerzy's left-handed power is what stands out the most, as he consistently squares up the baseball. He's more power than hit, but it's easy power, and while he may never hit for a high average, the home run pop should play in games. His play behind the plate is a bit more crude. He has an average arm that's accurate, even though he needs to improve his footwork. His hands work decently, and he should become an adequate overall receiver in time. The D-backs let Yerzy jump over the rookie-level Arizona League to go to the Pioneer League for his debut, where he was teaming up to make a very good catching trio with fellow 2016 draftee Ryan January and Venezuelan prospect Jose Herrera.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 55 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Ecker couldn't crack Texas A&M's staff as a freshman, appearing just four times all season, but he earned the closer's role and held onto it as a sophomore and junior, saving 16 games combined. That landed him in the fifth round, where the Tigers gave him full pick value as a college reliever who could be quick to the big leagues. Ecker has done nothing but pitch out of a bullpen, and he'll continue to do so, but he actually has a starting pitcher's repertoire. He'll work with a 93-96 mph fastball in shorter stints, and he backs that up with a changeup that he throws with good deception and that has splitter action to it. Ecker has thrown both a true slider and more of a hybrid breaking ball, and both have been average pitches. Not the biggest guy in the world, there was some concern about his longer arm action, but he has never been hit well. He might not be future big league closer material, but his stuff combined with his ability to throw strikes could allow him to move quickly and settle in as a Major League setup man down the road.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 60 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 A 17th-round pick out of high school by the Indians, Hendrix didn't get much work as a Texas A&M freshman, but he became nearly unhittable coming out of the bullpen as a sophomore last year. He continued to dominate for the first month of his junior season, putting himself in position to be one of the first relievers selected. A dip in velocity caused his stock to drop a bit, with the Reds nabbing him in the fifth round. Early in the year, Hendrix sat at 94-96 mph and reached 98 with his lively fastball. He worked more at 92-94 mph when he slumped, topping out at 97 on some days and just 92 on others. He had one of the best curveballs in the Draft, a power downer that can climb into the mid 80s, though it too was less sharp in the latter part of the season. Hendrix also has a changeup with some sink and deception, but he's likely a reliever long-term because of command and delivery concerns. The Reds kept him in the bullpen, and he advanced to full-season ball during his summer debut.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Early in 2016, May looked like the best high school pitching prospect in Texas after Forrest Whitley (who went 17th overall to the Astros) and Kyle Muller (who got first-round money in the second round from the Braves). May's velocity and stock dipped as the Draft approached, though he still commanded a $1 million bonus from the Dodgers as a third-rounder. He was the first player ever selected out of Northwest High (Justin, Texas), the alma mater of big leaguer Tyler Collins. After working with a low-80s fastball as a sophomore, May picked up velocity as he began to mature physically. He now operates at 90-93 mph and can peak at 95, and he could throw harder in the future because he still has a lot of projection remaining on his gangly 6-foot-6 frame. He generates high spin rates on his heater, giving it riding life that helps it avoid barrels. May also has shown high spin rates on his curveball in the past, though he has had more success with a harder slider that he added last spring. His changeup is in its nascent changes and doesn't have enough separation in velocity from his fastball yet. While he has a slingy delivery, it didn't prevent him from filling the strike zone in his pro debut.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Kessinger is trying to become the third member of his family to play in the big leagues, following his grandfather, Don (a six-time All-Star with the Cubs), and uncle, Keith. Seen as more of a steady player with so-so tools in his first two seasons at Mississippi, he hit .405 in Southeastern Conference play last spring and propelled himself into the second round of the 2019 Draft. Signed for a below-slot $750,000, he spent most of his pro debut in Class A. Though Kessinger has a track record of making repeated contact with a controlled right-handed swing and a line-drive approach, he was just a career .248 hitter with the Rebels before SEC play began last March. He started hitting the ball with more authority last spring, and the Astros like his bat speed and believe he can tap into more power if he gets his front foot down quicker. His patience enhances his on-base ability and he makes the most of his fringy speed on the bases. While Kessinger lacks quick-twitch actions and flash, and his arm is just average, he makes plays at shortstop thanks to his knack for positioning himself and his high baseball IQ. Most scouts believe he's destined for second base, though Houston is more optimistic and will keep him at short as long as possible. He might be more utilityman than regular, but his makeup will allow him to maximize his modest tools.

scouting_grades_text: Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 60 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40
bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 30 | Run: 60 | Arm: 45 | Field: 50 | Overall: 40 The last outfielder from Brigham Young University to spend any time in the big leagues was Jaycob Brigman, who was up with the A's for 48 games in 2017. Lund, taken by the Angels in the 11th round of the 2016 Draft, hopes to be the next after reaching Double-A in his first full season, then spending the year there in 2018. Lund is the type who gets the complimentary label from evaluators as being a "baseball player." At his best, he's a table-setting type who gets on base and uses his legs to help his team win. He still strikes out a bit too much, but he did draw walks in 2018 and can shoot line drives to all fields with a flat swing path, albeit without any real power. He's stolen 20 or more bases two years in a row and that should continue to be a big part of his game. He can handle all three outfield positions capably and is fine in center field, the spot he's played most frequently. Center field would be the only spot in the outfield Lund could play full-time. That spot is occupied at the moment in Los Angeles, which is fine because Lund profiles much better as a fourth outfielder.

bio_text: 2016 Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 The nephew of former big league catcher Rey Palacios, Joshua couldn't make Xavieran High's (Brooklyn) team as a sophomore but emerged as the 2013 New York City Player of the Year as a senior at the crosstown High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology. He spent the fall of his freshman college season at Stony Brook before transferring to San Jacinto (Texas) JC and turning down the Reds as a 31st-round pick in 2014. After moving on to Auburn this spring, he was hitting .408 and challenging for the Southeastern Conference batting title before injuring his right wrist diving for a ball in early April. Impressed with what he showed before the injury, the Blue Jays drafted Palacios in the fourth round and signed him for pick value. A switch-hitter in high school who hit exclusively left-handed in college, Palacios has a quick swing and makes consistent hard contact. He manages the strike zone well and focuses on producing line drives, while showing occasional power to his pull side. Most scouts grade Palacios as a plus runner, though some rate him closer to average, and he can steal a few bases. He tried catching at San Jacinto before settling in the outfield, and he played left field this spring at Auburn in deference to speedster Anfernee Grier in center. The Blue Jays are hopeful that Palacios can stick in center field, where his speed and average arm strength are clean fits, though some evaluators believe his instincts ultimately will land him back in left.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 The best position prospect to come out of Douglas High (Parkland, Fla.) since Anthony Rizzo, Welker led the Eagles to their first-ever state championship this spring even though they lost ace Jesus Luzardo to Tommy John surgery. The Rockies moved him from shortstop to third base after signing him in the fourth round for $855,000, and one club official said Welker reminded him of a young Nolan Arenado. An advanced hitter for a teenager, Welker has the potential to hit for power and average. He recognizes pitches well, has nice feel for the barrel and uses the entire field. He has good bat speed and leverage in his right-handed swing that should translate into home run pop as he gets stronger. Though Welker has below-average speed, he has good instincts on the bases and in the field. He took to the hot corner immediately and has the arm strength and accuracy to make all the plays there.
