bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Sands’ older brother, Carson, was a 2014 fourth-round pick of the Cubs out of high school. Cole opted to head to Florida State rather than sign in 2015 as a 22nd-round pick of the Astros. He’s been a three-year member of the Seminoles’ rotation and stepped into the Friday night role when Tyler Holton went down with an injury, though he missed some time with biceps tendinitis. Assuming health, and Sands was back on the mound in May, the right-hander has a solid three-pitch mix coming from a high three-quarter delivery and easy arm action. He’ll throw his fastball in the 92-95 mph range with good sink. His 80-83 mph slider is inconsistent, but it has sharp break and he can land it for strikes when it’s on. His changeup should be a third average offering, a solid offspeed pitch with good sink to it as well. Sands doesn’t miss a ton of bats, but goes right after hitters. He did pitch well on the Cape in brief performances for two summers, which certainly won’t hurt his chances of getting drafted in the top five rounds.

He had fringy fastball and lacked projection, however, so teams weren't willing to pay him enough to divert him from a Louisiana State commitment. Three years later, he still exudes pitchability and lacks wow velocity, though now he should go around the third round. The scouting report on Marceaux is pretty much the same as it was in high school, with his best pitch still a solid upper-70s curveball with downer break. He has added a tick or two of velocity to his fastball, which sits around 90-92 mph, touches 94 and plays up because of some running action and his ability to command it. He also has a low-80s slider that sometimes is more effective than his curve and a fading changeup with similar velocity. A student of the game, Marceaux understands how to tunnel and sequence his pitches to keep hitters off balance. He pounds the strike zone by repeating his low-effort delivery and employs a high three-quarters arm slot to overcome his lack of size and create downhill plane on his pitches. He's a high-floor prospect with a good chance to become a No. 4 or 5 starter, and perhaps more than that if he can find some more velocity as a pro.

bio_text: 2018 Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 50 | Arm: 70 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Alexander's father, Chuck, pitched in the Indians system for parts of four seasons. Blaze has plenty of arm strength, but his future is as an infielder. A big summer on the showcase circuit put him high on follow lists, and while an uneven spring caused his stock to fall a little, the D-backs saw enough to take him in the 11th round and give him an above-pick-value bonus of $500,000 to sign him away from his South Carolina commitment. It starts with his arm, which grades out as an 80 in terms of pure strength, though he'll need to work on accuracy with his throws across the diamond. He has good enough hands and range to stay at shortstop long-term. This spring, there were more questions about his bat. He has some raw power and bat speed, but there was enough swing-and-miss to worry some scouts about how his bat will translate at the next level, though he got off to a good start during his pro debut in the rookie-level Arizona League. Clearly the D-backs feel good about Alexander being able to continue to hit and become an all-around shortstop, even if it takes a while. If all else fails, he can always follow in his dad's footsteps to the mound, where he was 93-95 mph as a raw thrower in high school.

Sharts has a three-pitch mix and isn’t afraid to throw any of them. He’s been largely in the 90-92 mph range now, though some have seen him up to 94 mph, jumping from 85-88 mph as a junior thanks to an extensive offseason workout regimen. His 72-75 mph curve could be a Major League average pitch in the future, but it’s his changeup that’s his better secondary pitch, an 82-84 mph offspeed pitch that has the chance to be plus. The best player to come out of Simi Valley High School in terms of big league impact has been a pitcher, Scott Radinsky. Sharts doesn’t project to go as early as Radinsky’s second-round selection in 1986, but he could go in the top five rounds, becoming the first in his high school to get taken since 2009.

His fastball sits in the low 90s, has touched higher at times, with some good life down in the zone. He has good feel for his breaking ball, a curve that should be a least an average secondary pitch for him. His changeup is very much a work in progress and it’s not a pitch he uses in games. Despite some issues with his delivery and arm action, Champlain is a decent strike thrower, but he has a way to go to develop from thrower to pitcher. Signability could be a concern, with a spot at Southern California waiting should he go the college route.

With a strong spring, Wright has been grabbing some of that spotlight as he aims to become the first pitcher drafted from the school. There’s a lot to like in this 6-foot-5 right-hander’s stuff, starting with his pure arm strength. Wright has been up to 96 mph at times this spring, though he usually sits in the 91-92 mph range and hasn’t always held his velocity deep into his starts. He doesn’t always use his lower half effectively and doing so should allow him to maintain his velo. He throws an average slider that has three-quarter tilt to it when it’s on, but often looks more like a hard slurve. Like many high school pitchers, his changeup is developing. Size and arm strength can’t be taught and both are boxes scouts check off when it comes to Wright. Some mechanical adjustments could help him take off at the next level, with perhaps enough to work with to sign him away from his Louisville commitment.

Goss (a 2019 supplemental first-round pick by the Rays) and Matt Thompson (a 2019 second-rounder by the White Sox). Madden should go higher than either of them in 2021 because his stuff and command have continually improved in college. The Big 12 Conference pitcher of the year, he could become the first Longhorns hurler selected in the first 10 picks since Kevin Garner in 1987. Madden topped out at 95 mph in high school and now operates at 93-96 with sink and bore on his fastball after reaching 99 mph during the fall. His best offering at Cypress Ranch was his slider, which has gained velocity and arrives in the mid-80s with late bite. His fading low-80s changeup gives him a solid third offering and he also can mix in an upper-70s curveball with depth but less consistency than his slider. Madden added 35 pounds to his 6-foot-3 frame in college and the extra strength has helped him not only to improve his pitches but also to repeat his sound delivery more consistently. He walked just four batters in four starts last spring and scouts love the way he attacks hitters. He has the ingredients to become a frontline starter.

He hit safely in his first 18 starts and has performed steadily ever since for the Owls and during two summers in the Cape Cod League. He's not loaded with sexy tools but he's a grinder who gets the most out of what he has. Proctor uses a compact left-handed stroke to drill line drives to all fields. He controls the strike zone well and projects to post solid batting averages and on-base percentages. While he won't be a slugger, he does have a bit of raw power and is doing a better job of driving the ball in 2018. Proctor's fringy speed and quickness limits his effectiveness on the bases and range at shortstop. He has the hands and actions for the position, but he possesses just an average arm and can't always make plays to his right. Though he'll get the chance to stick at shortstop in pro ball, he's likely destined for second base.

Any team considering Delgado in the top five or so rounds will be doing so because of the bat and the hopes of figuring out his position down the road. Whether or not he can be signed away from his Florida International commitment remains to be seen.

As a sophomore, he was a swingman, then had an outstanding showing in the Cape Cod League over the summer. That catapulted him into the Wildcats’ Friday night role, where he’s been a solid performer this spring. The 6-foot-3 right-hander has a three-pitch mix that could give him the chance to start as a pro. He’ll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range, though it’s fairly straight. His out pitch is his 79-83 mph curve, a plus breaking ball he can land for strikes, and he mixes in an average changeup effectively. While he doesn’t have pinpoint command, he is generally around the strike zone and competes like a closer every time he’s on the mound. Deason has proven he can handle starting and any team taking him will likely send him out in that role until he proves he can’t handle it. His stuff will tick up in shorter relief stints, and some scouts do see him as a seventh or eighth inning setup man when all is said and done.

This spring, Gerber matched Jay by the end of the regular season and also climbed to within two of his Illini career mark of 24 saves. Though he didn't go as high in the Draft as Jay, Gerber's impressive career still netted him a sixth-round selection and $167,400 signing bonus in June. A pure reliever who has never started a game in three years of college or during summer ball, Gerber attacks hitters with two pitches. He has sat at 92-96 mph with his fastball throughout the spring, even when working on consecutive days. Gerber's sharp 82-85 mph slider can be a plus pitch at times and is especially tough on right-handers. Gerber has a lot of flying parts in his funky delivery, which provides deception but also hampers his command at times. How well he can locate his pitches ultimately will determine if he reaches his ceiling as a set-up man. Gerber's strong 6-foot-4 frame and resilient arm make him a durable bullpen option, and he should be one of the first 2018 draftees to reach the big leagues.

He served as a mid-week starter for part of his freshman year before finding his niche as the Tigers' closer the last two seasons. He didn't allowed an earned run as Team USA's co-closer last summer and surrendered just three during the regular season this spring. Though he's just 5-foot-10, Gilliam has a quick arm that produces 91-96 mph fastballs. His curveball gives him a second plus pitch, arriving in the upper 70s with 12-to-6 action. He also has an effective changeup from his days as a starter, though he doesn't use it much as a reliever. Gilliam works with a high-tempo delivery that adds some funk but also makes it difficult to control his offerings at times. He's a good athlete, which reduces some of the durability concerns that his size creates. Though he has three pitches, he projects strictly as a reliever and could advance quickly through the Minors.

A team that believes Little can handle a more challenging position than left field could pop him in the third round. With Little's simple approach and advanced feel for hitting, he makes consistent hard contact to all fields from the right side of the plate. He has significantly increased his power output as a sophomore and has enough strength and bat speed to provide 30 doubles and 15 homers per season as a pro. He manages the strike zone well and has solid speed on the basepaths. Little has spent most of his college career in left field because the Red Raiders have a superior defender in Cody Farhat in center. Some scouts think Little has the quickness to play center and would give him the chance to do so at the next level. Texas Tech tried him at shortstop in fall ball, and while his below-average arm wasn't a good fit there, he intrigues some evaluators as a possible second baseman.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 45 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Vavra comes from a baseball family that includes a father (Joe) who has spent 37 seasons in pro ball and currently serves the Tigers as a quality control coach, plus two older brothers (Tanner and Trey) who reached Class A in the Twins' system. The best prospect among them, Terrin earned consensus first-team All-America recognition after batting .386/.455/.664 at Minnesota this spring. A third-round pick who signed for $550,000, Vavra continued to hit in his pro debut. A stress fracture in his back truncated his freshman season and continued to bothered him as a sophomore, but Vavra finally is showing what he's capable of offensively now that he's fully healthy. He makes repeated line-drive contact with ease, thanks to his smooth left-handed stroke and advanced approach. He also has some sneaky raw power and could hit 15 homers per season as a pro. Scouts rave about Vavra's baseball IQ and makeup as much as his tools. He's just an average runner out of the batter's box but is quicker underway and his instincts help him make things happen on the bases and in the field. He doesn't have the plus range and arm teams want at shortstop, so he might wind up as an offensive second baseman.

Concussions kept him off the field for much of his first two years, but he burst onto the radar with a healthy, and huge, junior season in 2018, when he led Division I hitters in slugging percentage, OPS, while hitting 22 homers through the regular season. The Reds liked his potential with the bat enough to take him in the third round, signing him for below pick value and sending him to the Pioneer League for his pro debut. Spillane has both strength and leverage in his frame, and he combines it well with his bat speed to produce his plus raw power. He showed the ability to drive balls to all fields in college, though it remains to be seen if he'll be able to turn on good pro inside fastballs. There is some length to his swing, so strikeouts will always be a part of his game and he did strike out 41 percent of the time during his summer debut. He does offset that with an ability to draw walks, but he will likely continue to be a power over hit offensive player. A first baseman in college, Spillane is a good athlete and he saw more time in right field than first base during his first summer with the Reds. He could profile as an everyday right fielder if he hits enough and taps into his power consistently.

But he has confounded scouts by not making more progress offensively, and they now wonder if his defense might be better than his bat. He still shows decent potential both ways, which along with his track record will make him one of the first backstops selected. Koch's raw power is his best offensive trait, the product of strength and good-not-great bat speed, though there are questions as to how consistently he'll get to it in pro ball. He looks to crush everything to his pull side, leaving him vulnerable on the outer half of the plate. He has managed the strike zone well in college but his approach could get exploited by pro pitchers. Koch has made strides behind the plate this spring, cleaning up his receiving and improving his framing skills. He has average arm strength that plays up a bit because he gets rid of the ball quickly and makes accurate throws. He does a nice job of running a pitching staff.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 55 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Rivas went undrafted after a solid high school career in La Jolla, Calif., but a lot has changed during his three years at Arizona. A three-year starter, two spent as a two-way player, Rivas' bat really started coming around as a sophomore. After focusing solely on his hitting as a junior, he became the A's fourth-round pick in June, signed for $446,500 and then had a strong pro debut in the New York-Penn League. The left-handed hitter's calling card is his bat. He can flat-out hit and makes a ton of contact at the plate while showing solid on-base skills. The one knock on Rivas offensively has been his power, which hasn't shown up consistently from his solid 6-foot frame. Some think the power will eventually come, and that will be important for him to profile at a corner position. He primarily plays first base, and has good footwork, solid hands and an above-average arm there, but he's also played the outfield and might prefer playing right field if given the choice. In either spot, Rivas' ability to be a run producer will be important for him to profile as an everyday player there. Given his strengths as a hitter, Rivas could move relatively quickly through the Minors, especially if his power emerges as the A's hope it will.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 55 | Run: 50 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 There are three players from New York in MLB Pipeline’s Draft Top 200 this year. Mack is the lone hitter of the trio, with enough thump in the bat to interest teams in the top five or six rounds, albeit without a sure-fire defensive home. Mack is stocky and physical at 5-foot-11, but athletic enough to play shortstop capably for his high school team. Few see him sticking at the position, however, because he’s a bit heavy-legged in terms of his range and while he does have some arm strength, he doesn’t always show the ability to throw from different arm angles, a skill needed for the premium position. A move to second might work, with others suggesting third or left field, where his arm would probably play up to average. Playing a corner spot would put more pressure on his bat, and there is some serious raw power for him to tap into. That power, and the hope he’ll hit enough to get to it consistently, is what teams will be banking on should they take the left-handed hitter. Whether a team likes it enough to lure him away from his Clemson commitment remains to be seen.

Richie has made a name for himself as a three-year starter at Towson and one of the better performers in the Colonial Athletic Association. A left-handed hitter who plays shortstop for Towson, Palacios could be a favorite of the analytics set because of his outstanding on base skills and his fairly consistent performance with the bat. He has walked far more often than he has struck out and that, along with his excellent speed, makes him a potential table-setter in the future. There is some raw power to tap into, though it’s not a huge part of his game. Stealing bases is and he has been very efficient on that front. Defensively, some see a move off of shortstop, mostly because his fringy arm won’t play there. Second base or perhaps even center field might be a better fit. A team taking Palacios in the first five rounds will be banking on his bat and on-base skills translating to the pro level. His brother Josh was taken in the fourth round of the 2016 Draft, 132nd overall, so there could be some family bragging rights on the line.

Based on talent, Song should go way before that, though the military obligations a Naval Academy student has could keep that from happening. Navy’s ace has a strong track record of performance with the kind of stuff and 6-foot-4 frame that looks like a future starting pitcher. He’s shown a strong arm and a solid fastball that will touch as high as 96 mph at timemes. The rest of his stuff is average across the board, though he’ll flash above-average breaking stuff at times. He generally throws strikes, but his overall command fluctuates. A team taking Song in the early rounds of the Draft will be buying the arm strength and the belief that his secondary stuff will continue to come, making him a solid big league starter. That team will also have to be willing to go through the arduous task of finding a way to get him signed given his military commitment.

But the speedy outfielder has shown enough where teams that covet college performers will still have interest in the top five rounds It’s not that Artis, a two-time Cape Cod League player, has been bad this spring; it’s just that he set the bar high by winning the Big South Conference’s Freshman of the Year in 2016 and then Player of the Year in 2017. He’s proven he can really hit, albeit from an unorthodox crouch from the left side of the plate. There is some raw power, but he doesn’t tap into it consistently, focusing on line-drive contact and drawing a lot more walks than strikeouts. He’s a plus runner who can handle center field with below-average arm strength, one who could one day hit near the top of a big league lineup. Even in his “down year,” Artis has gotten on base at an impressive clip and stolen bases. That skill set, not to mention his track record, has kept him fairly high on Draft boards.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 70 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 40 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 Montes de Oca remains one of the biggest enigmas in the Draft, perhaps the biggest. He had Tommy John surgery as a Missouri high school junior in 2013 and ulnar nerve transposition three years later, and he turned down the White Sox as a 14th-rounder in 2014 and the Nationals as a 15th-rounder last summer. While all that is off-putting to a lot of teams, when he's on he might have the most devastating pair of pitches available in this year's crop. Montes de Oca can work at 93-98 mph and reach 100 with exceptionally heavy sink on his fastball, which can get top-of-the-scale grades for both its velocity and its life. His breaking ball has gone from a power slurve to more of a true slider that climbs into the upper 80s and is a wipeout offering at its best. Both pitches were overpowering when he worked the first seven innings of a no-hitter against Maryland-Baltimore County in March, when he struck out 12 of the 23 batters he faced and permitted just two balls to be hit in the air. After continuing to excel in the rotation over the next month, Montes de Oca pitched just 11 innings over the final seven weeks of the regular season without any explanation as to why his role changed. His lack of a reliable changeup and his inability to throw consistent strikes point to a future in the bullpen. With his stuff, he could move rapidly as a reliever and have closer upside if he stays healthy.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 After getting shelled by Virginia Military in his first 2018 start, Hill flirted with no-hitters against Charleston Southern and Clemson in his next two outings while striking out 14 each time. That sent his Draft stock soaring, though he hasn't been as sharp since and missed a start in March with shoulder tendinitis. He still has a chance to become the fourth South Carolina right-hander selected in the top three rounds in the last three Drafts, following Clarke Schmidt, Wil Crowe and Braden Webb. Hill's best pitch is his fastball, which sits around 91-93 mph and peaks at 95. He uses his 6-foot-5 frame to create good plane and extension, and has some crossfire in his delivery that imparts running life on his heater. His changeup has been more reliable than his slider this spring, with each showing signs of becoming a solid offering when at their best. Hill is more physical than athletic, and he sometimes struggles to keep his delivery together and locate his pitches where he wants. If he can do a better job of maintaining his velocity into the later innings, improving the consistency of his secondary offerings and commanding his stuff, he could be a No. 3 starter. If not, he might be more of a sixth- or seventh-inning reliever because he lacks an overpowering fastball or a dynamic second pitch.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 65 | Curveball: 60 | Control: 40 | Overall: 45 An Arizona high school product who originally committed to North Carolina, Dillard wound up at San Jacinto (Texas) JC instead, making him Draft-eligible as a freshman this spring. He and McLennan (Texas) CC catcher/right-hander Josh Breaux excited scouts when they both hit 98 mph while facing each other on Feb. 9, but both have pitched sparingly since while dealing with elbow issues. Dillard has added significant physical strength in the last year, boosting his fastball from 88-92 mph as a prep starter to 93-98 mph as a JUCO reliever. His breaking ball has gotten quicker as well, becoming a power slurve with curveball break and slider velocity at 82-86 mph. As impressive as his pure stuff is, he requires a lot of polish. Dillard has a faster-paced tempo and some effort in his delivery that adds deception but also leads to unreliable command and control. If he can stay healthy and do a better job of locating his pitches, he could become a high-leverage reliever. He has committed to Missouri for 2019 if he doesn't turn pro this summer.

Other college hitters in the area may have passed him, but he was coming on strong as the Draft approached. Keirsey has excellent bat to ball skills and makes consistent hard contact. It’s more of a line drive approach at present, though the left-handed hitter has some extra-base thump. The more Keirsey looks like his pre-injury self, the more his name was moving up boards, with some buzz as early as the third round. Chicago agreed, drafting him in the second round this June and signing him for $1.1 million. Davis' signature tool is plus-plus speed that could make him a devastating basestealer and quality center fielder once he improves his reads and instincts. While he has a huge ceiling, Davis also will need plenty of time to develop. He has improved his right-handed swing, but he still has more adjustments to make and also must hone his pitch recognition and plate discipline. The amount of progress he has made since focusing on baseball leads to optimism that he'll figure things out offensively.

He recovered to go on a tear as the Draft approached, hitting his way into the second round and a $1.1 million bonus from the Mariners. After his steady pro debut, Seattle swapped him to the Yankees in January for second-base prospect Shed Long, who had just been acquired from the Reds along with a 2019 Competitive Balance A Draft pick in exchange for Sonny Gray and left-handed pitching prospect Reiver Sanmartin. Stowers took off once he smoothed out his right-handed stroke and took a more direct path to the ball. He's at his best when he tries to hit line drives to all fields, and while he isn't a power hitter, he has enough pop to produce 12-15 homers per year as a pro. Stowers has an extremely patient approach and a knack for stealing bases. Scouts give Stowers solid-to-plus grades for his speed, yet there's mixed opinion on whether he can stick in center field at the next level. It's essential that he does so to profile as a regular, because he doesn't have the power to profile on a corner. Stowers' below-average arm will push him to left field if he can't stay in center.

He also led the Hawkeyes in hitting (.387) at the World University Games in August and has set career bests nearly across the board this spring. Neustrom's most attractive tool is his power potential, the product of strength, solid bat speed and loft in his left-handed swing. There are times when he focuses on using the opposite field, and others when he gets pull-happy and vulnerable on the other half. He makes consistent contact and draws his share of walks. While Neustrom is slow out of the box, he moves well for a 6-foot-3, 210-pounder and has at least average speed once he gets going. He plays right field for Iowa and possesses an average arm, though most scouts project him as a left fielder in pro ball. He needs to improve his reads and routes as a defender, and he has the work ethic to get the job done.

Kinneman's speed and arm elicit grades from fringy to solid. A team that believes he's on the high end of that range could try him in right field, though he has played in left at North Carolina State. He's a respectable athlete but most of his value will come from his bat.

His changeup wasn't quite as deceptive as it had been previously, though he has the makings of an average third offering. Bartnicki has a strong frame and the athleticism to throw strikes, though his control also has wavered this year. His delivery is clean but also somewhat slow and gives batters a good look at his pitches. He has a ceiling as a mid-rotation starter but will need plenty of patience and development to get there.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 35 | Arm: 45 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 Raleigh comes from a baseball family, with a father and uncle who both played at Western Carolina. His dad went on to coach at his alma mater and at Tennessee, while his uncle spent 10 years in the Minor Leagues. The younger Raleigh jumped on the map as a freshman at Florida State, scuffled as a sophomore, but bounced back with a strong junior season, hitting 13 home runs and while pacing the Seminoles in batting (.326), hits (75), RBIs (54) and slugging (.583). A dearth of college catchers further pushed him up teams' Draft boards, and the Mariners were pleased to find him available ahead of their third-round pick. The switch-hitting backstop swung the bat well in the second half of his junior season, using an advanced approach at the plate to hit for average and power while drawing a ton of walks. It's a power-over-hit profile from both sides of the plate, though some question whether Raleigh will hit enough at the next level to tap consistently into that raw pop. His defensive game, however, lags behind his bat. The big-bodied catcher lacks agility behind the plate, with blocking, receiving and catch-and-throw skills that leave something to be desired. College catching is always hard to find, and Raleigh did it for three years at Florida State. His bat is his calling card to the Major Leagues and gives him a chance to develop into a offensive-minded backstop if can also make gains on the other side of the ball.

With a durable frame, good athleticism and the ability to repeat his deliberate delivery, he's equipped to be a starter. He'll need to avoid nibbling at the plate and challenge hitters more consistently, and has made progress in that regard since signing.

They've blossomed into two of the more dependable starters in power conferences, with Hjelle a possible first-rounder out of Kentucky and Irvin likely to go in the first five rounds. He moved into Oklahoma's rotation midway through his freshman season and has been a mainstay ever since, with the exception of missing two starts with shoulder inflammation as a sophomore. Though he looks the part of a power pitcher at an athletic 6-foot-6 and 225 pounds, Irvin doesn't have overpowering stuff. His fastball parks at 90-92 mph and peaks at 95, featuring armside run and a bit of sink. He relies heavily on his heater and a short slider in the low 80s, rarely using his serviceable changeup. Though he has a long arm action that can affect the consistency of his secondary pitches, Irvin has improved his control and command throughout his college career. There's little effort in his delivery and he repeats it well. His stuff may be as good as it's going to get, making his floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter or middle reliever stand out more than his ceiling.

He enjoyed similar success as a sophomore before missing nearly two months with shoulder tendinitis, then got off to a brilliant start this year only to fade in late April. Scouts aren't sure exactly what to make of a guy they projected as a second- or third-rounder coming into 2018. While Martin doesn't have a true plus pitch, he knows how to mix two versions of a fastball and two effective secondary offerings. He'll usually work with a sinking two-seam fastball at 89-92 mph, though he can reach back for a mid-90s four-seamer a couple of times per game. His tight slider is usually his best secondary pitch, though some scouts prefer his changeup, which he'll throw in any count. Martin has a strong frame that lends itself more to durability than projection. He usually pounds the strike zone, though his control and command deserted him toward the end of the regular season. Scouts love his mound presence and guile, and he'll catch unsuspecting hitters off guard by quick-pitching them.

Campbell has all the tools to succeed behind the plate. He receives and blocks well, and he makes accurate throws with solid arm strength. He plays with energy and has admirable leadership skills. Campbell has played through a hamate injury that has hampered him at the plate this spring. His strength stands out more than his bat speed, though his right-handed swing is quick enough. He currently employs a middle-away approach that's more conducive to hitting for average than power, though he could have more pop once he starts to turn on more pitches.

He has legitimate right-handed power coming from a strong, athetic body. He’s more strength over bat speed with a bit of an uphill swing, something he’ll likely need to shorten to ensure he taps into that raw pop consistently at the next level. A below-average runner, there are some questions about his ability to stay at the hot corner because of his hands and lack of range. He is fairly physically mature. There were several teams looking at Guilbe in the top five rounds. Those are the teams that believe his bat will translate and he’ll hit enough to make his power a plus tool and make it worthwhile to lure him away from his University of Tennessee commitment.

Though he's one of college baseball hardest-throwing starters, he hasn't had nearly the same success during three years at Ohio State. His fastball velocity and performance in college baseball's top summer league could still get him drafted in the first five rounds, however. Feltner has been clocked as high as 98 mph and can carry a 93-95 mph fastball deep into games, with good downhill plane and some armside run. His changeup can be a plus pitch at times, featuring deceptive arm speed as well as fade. He flashed an improved slider on the Cape last summer but lacks feel to spin and has pitched with a below-average breaking ball for much of 2018. While Feltner generates premium starter velocity without much effort, hitters see the ball well against him and don't miss his fastball as much as would be expected. His control and command lack consistency, which also makes him vulnerable. The consensus is that he's best suited for a relief role as a pro, and he could have a plus-plus heater in shorter stints.

But that has been enough to attract scouts, because he has hit 98 mph as a rare Draft-eligible redshirt freshman. Schaller has worked at 95-98 mph in short stints, generating velocity without much effort. He'll occasionally throw some sharp mid-80s sliders, but for the most part his breaking ball has been below average. He has used his changeup so infrequently that it's best described as a work in progress. Though he has thrown strikes, Schaller has been hit harder than expected for someone with a mid-90s fastball. He needs to improve his command and his secondary pitches to keep batters off his heater. He's far from a finished product and his signability is uncertain, but his fastball alone makes him intriguing.

Smith not only is poised to become the first draftee since then, but also the first one ever with the potential to go in the top 10 rounds. The first thing that stands out about Smith is his size, and it’s something that came late to him. The right-hander was reportedly 6-foot-3 and throwing in the low-80s at the end of high school. Now he’s 6-foot-10 and has added a lot of velocity, throwing his fastball up to 97 mph consistently. Because he hasn’t always thrown that hard, Smith has an idea of how to pitch, mixing in his secondary offerings effectively, flashing average sliders and changeups. While he comes across his body with his short-strided delivery, the ball comes out of his hand clean and easy, and he’s thrown strikes this year. Smith has become one of the most intriguing Draft prospects in the Pacific Northwest, if not the country. It’s hard to know exactly what he’ll become, but he’s moved himself firmly into Day 2 Draft status, with teams likely to want to give Smith the chance to figure it out in their system.

He made up for his lost year by leading the Horizon League with a 2.13 ERA and winning conference freshman of the year honors in 2017. He also pitched well in the Cape Cod League last summer and has continued to thrive as a redshirt sophomore this spring, cementing his status as the Raiders' best pitching prospect since Joe Smith was a Mets third-rounder in 2006. The owner of a mid-80s fastball in high school, Weiss now operates at 91-93 mph and can hit 96 with his fastball. His heater can get fairly straight but arrives on a steep downhill plane because he's 6-foot-4 and employs a nearly overhand delivery. He throws his changeup with the same arm speed and it shows flashes of becoming a solid pitch with some fade and sink. Weiss' curveball isn't as reliable as his other offerings but has the makings of an average third pitch. He fills the strike zone but will need to command his pitches better at the next level. Scouts like his mound presence and envision him becoming a No. 4 or 5 starter.

He didn't back that up during his senior year, causing some teams to back off. The Mets weren't one of them, remembering his summer dominance when they took him in the second round and giving him an above-pick-value bonus of $1.85 million to sign him away from his Texas commitment. Over the summer, Woods-Richardson ran his fastball up to 95 mph and showed three-pitch potential. During his senior year, he sat more around 89-92 mph with his fastball, though scouts still loved his arm speed and athleticism. His curve wasn't quite as sharp as it was over the summer and he didn't used his changeup as much during his high school season. With a good delivery featuring a high-three-quarters arm slot, Woods-Richardson repeats his delivery well. He'll need to show he can maintain his stuff deep into his outings to show he can remain a starter long-term. A talented two-way player in high school, the Mets hope a focus on the mound will help him to put it all together in the future.

His father Justin played with current head coach Darin Erstad at Nebraska in 1995, and Colby gave the Cornhuskers a verbal commitment as a sophomore. Based on talent alone, he could crack the first five rounds. Gomes' fastball velocity fluctuated with the weather during an unusually cold spring, as he would pitch at 87-92 mph on some days and 91-95 on others, holding it deeper into games once it warmed up. He has some feel to spin a curveball with some power and depth, though it lacks consistency. He can throw his changeup for strikes but needs to refine it further. Gomes has a long, lanky frame with plenty of projection remaining. He's athletic and does a nice job of maintaining his three-quarters arm slot. If it doesn't happen this year, he could be an early-round choice in 2021 after three years of adding polish at Nebraska.

It's true again this spring with Halvorsen, which may make him follow through on a commitment to Missouri. He wants to play shortstop and pro teams clearly prefer him on the mound. Halvorsen throws harder than most high schoolers, hitting 96 mph while earning a save in the Perfect Game All-American Classic last August and pumping the second-quickest fastball (95.4 mph) at the World Wood Bat Assocation World Championship last October. Though horrible weather this spring delayed his senior season until mid-April, he regularly threw 92-95 once he took the mound. He generates his velocity with arm speed rather than effort and has some armside run on his heater. Halvorsen has decent feel for his curveball and changeup but both are works in progress because he has spent more time on his development as a position player. He threw a slider last summer, which some scouts preferred to his curve. He has the raw power, arm strength and athleticism to profile as a college third baseman but won't get the opportunity to hit if he does turn pro.

The key to his success is a pitch he says he learned via the Internet. Wolf wanted to add a cut fastball while he was on the Cape last summer, so he googled "Mariano Rivera cutter" and now has a solid one that is his lone above-average offering. His 89-91 mph fastball tops out at 93 and plays up a little bit with some run and sink. He also has a curveball and a changeup that he can land for strikes, and he can morph his cutter into more of a slider. Wolf's 6-foot-6 frame and three-quarters arm slot create deceptive angle that adds to the effectiveness of his modest repertoire. He helps himself by controlling all of his pitches and doing little things like fielding his position well and controlling the running game. If he can't make it as a starter at the next level, he could have a future as a reliever because he's very tough on left-handers.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 60 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Sandlin recorded 20 saves in his first two seasons at Southern Mississippi and dealt in the Cape Cod League last summer, then shifted to the rotation this spring. The move couldn't have gone much better, as he ended the regular season leading NCAA Division I in WHIP (0.71) and ranking second in ERA (1.25). He has high spin rates on his pitches, making him even more attractive to analytically minded clubs. While he's a 5-foot-11 right-hander without overpowering stuff, he makes up for it by mixing five pitches and three arm angles. He'll throw a four-seam fastball and a curveball from a nearly overhand slot and a two-seamer and a slider as a sidearmer, and he'll also work in a changeup and a lower-three-quarters angle. It all adds up to about a dozen combinations of pitches and slots, and he can hit 94 mph with nasty life on his fastball from down low. Sandlin will have to tighten his slider at the next level, because pro hitters won't chase it as much as collegians do. He has the makings of a solid changeup too, and his feel for altering speeds and eye levels while pounding the strike zone gives him the opportunity to continue to succeed as a starter at the next level. His size will lead to durability questions -- he left one April start early and missed the next with shoulder stiffness -- and a pro team could be tempted to move him quickly as a reliever.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 There are some real high school baseball powers in Florida. Nature Coast Technical High School, where Gates pitches and hits, is not one of them, but Gates made a name for himself by pitching well at a number of showcase events last summer. While Gates plays two ways in high school, his future is most certainly on the mound. The left-hander is fairly physically mature, with a three-pitch mix he uses well. His fastball this spring has been in the 88-91 mph range, sometimes touching a tick higher. He throws a solid breaking ball that sometimes has slider shape and some see more as a power curve and he has shown the ability to throw a changeup with good arm speed. There is some effort in his delivery, which can impact his overall command, and there is a debate about whether his future is as a starter or reliever, where his plus competitiveness would be an asset. A team taking him in the top five or six rounds and signing him away from his Miami commitment will give him every chance to stick in a rotation.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 Carranza spent the first two years of his college career at Oregon, but transferred to Division II Asuza Pacific for his junior season. After a strong showing in the Northwoods League over the summer, he has stepped in as the Cougars’ ace and has helped them be one of the top DII teams in the country. Now 6-foot-5, Carranza has some projection, with the chance to add velocity as he adds strength to his frame. He’s already up to 95 mph with his fastball and comfortably sits around 92 mph. His low-80s slider is inconsistent, but shows depth and tilt enough to make you think it can be an average pitch in the future. He’ll flash a solid changeup with fade on occasion as well. Carranza has missed bats this year at a good clip, but command has eluded him, both in and out of the strike zone, leading to a high walk rate and getting hit more than he should. Still, his live arm and good frame could point to a future in the back of a rotation, enough for a team to consider him in the top six rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 40 | Arm: 60 | Field: 60 | Overall: 45 There are college catchers who can really hit, but might have to move out from behind the plate because of their defensive inefficiencies. Then there are those like Meyer, who undoubtedly have a future as a defensive backstop, with how much they hit truly determining what kind of professional career they have. A three-year starter at Cal Poly, Meyer’s glove also earned him a spot on USA Baseball’s Collegiate National Team. He has excellent hands and moves well behind the plate, allowing him to receive and block well. He has a strong and accurate arm, recording excellent pop times to second base on a consistent basis. Offensively, the right-handed hitter has been less productive. He does make consistent contact and rarely strikes out with decent on-base skills. And he’s having his best offensive season now, albeit without any power. Meyer more than likely profiles as a backup at the next level. If his bat comes around with pro instruction, he could become a defensive-minded regular. In either case, his defensive skillset should have him off the board in the top six rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 45 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 It seems more often than not, prospects who play shortstop in college have to move to another position when they begin their pro careers. Pena is an exception to that rule as an infielder who definitely can stick at the premium position. How much a team believes he’ll hit will ultimately determine his Draft status. A product of the Providence, Rhode Island high school ranks who went on to the University of Maine, Pena profiles as a solid to plus defender who can play shortstop at any level. He has good speed that leads to excellent range and possesses the strong arm and footwork necessary to excel at the demanding spot. At the plate, Pena does have some strength and raw power, enough where some see 15 homers annually as a reasonable projection. But that’s only if he makes enough consistent contact to get to that power. There’s length to his right-handed swing, which leads to some swing and miss issues with an at times overly aggressive approach. Some of that can be corrected mechanically once he gets to pro ball, and shortening him up will likely be a primary objective for whatever team drafts him. With his defensive profile, being able to unlock a more consistent bat could produce an everyday big league shortstop.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 Plassmeyer quickly worked his way into Missouri's weekend rotation as a freshman in 2016 but pitched his way out of it midway the following year. After working during the offseason to add velocity to his fastball and sharpness to his slider, he rebounded to become the Tigers' best starter in ‘18. The Mariners made Plassmeyer their fourth-round pick that June, then traded him to Tampa Bay during the offseason along with Mike Zunino and Guillermo Heredia. He pitched his way from Class A Bowling Green up to Triple-A Durham in his first full season, finishing second in the Minors (120 IP min.) with a 1.91 ERA. Plassmeyer has below-average velocity on his fastball, which sits 89-90 mph and peaks at 93, but it plays as an above-average pitch because its high spin creates running action and he commands it so well. His slider is average, but he manages to sneak it by more hitters than would be expected. A changeup that has some late fade gives Plassmeyer a third average pitch that he threw with more confidence in 2019. He's not afraid to pitch inside despite lacking swing-and-miss stuff. Plassmeyer’s effectiveness is largely, if not entirely tied to his plus-plus control. After issuing 35 walks in 203 1/3 innings (1.5 BB/9) in three years at Missouri, he’s allowed 27 free passes across 156 frames (1.6 BB/9) as a pro. Plassmeyer’s stuff limits his ceiling, but he has a high floor as a back-of-the-rotation starter who will compete and gobble up innings.

The Yankees did take him in the 35th round in 2018 and he's now back as a Draft-eligible sophomore coming off a solid freshman season and very strong Cape Cod League showing. There is no question that Wells' bat plays. The left-handed hitter has power to all fields, with good timing and a simple setup at the plate. He has strength and bat speed and controls the bat head well to make loud contact. He does strike out a bit, but he also draws a lot of walks. There are more concerns about where he might play defensively. He's adequate behind the plate, and while his arm stroke and release are fine, his throws are inconsistent. He is a decent enough athlete to play first or figure things out in left field. A team taking Wells with its first pick might want to send him out as a catcher until he proves he can't play the position. His bat should play regardless of his eventual defensive position and he could end up following a Kyle Schwarber type path to the big leagues.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 It can be difficult for high school players from Hawaii to gain exposure, though Bello was seen at the Area Code Games last summer, Perfect Game’s WWBA World Championship in the fall, and also participated in a Prospect Development Pipeline event in Los Angeles in February. The upside of hailing from Hawaii? Getting to work out with the Cardinals’ Kolten Wong and his brother, Rays prospect Kean, during the offseason. Bello profiles as a top-of-the-order catalyst who can impact the game with his speed on both sides of the ball. The right-handed hitter makes consistent contact and projects to be an average hitter. He needs to add strength, but there is some extra-base pop in his swing. He has the kind of speed to steal bases and cover a lot of ground in the outfield, with the chance to be an above-average defender eventually, and a plus arm to boot. There hasn’t been a top five round pick from Hawaii since Ian Kahaloa went to the Reds in the fifth in 2015, and the last time a high school position player from there went that early was when the younger Wong brother joined Isiah Kiner-Falefa as fourth rounders in 2013. Bello, a St. Mary’s commit, has the chance to join that select group.

Scouts came to Redan this spring to check out speedy shortstop Kevin Smith and came away more impressed with Bradley, who entered 2018 more noted as a position player. Now his future clearly is on the mound, though the difference between his present and his projection may make him difficult to sign away from South Carolina. Bradley pitches at 88-91 mph and reaches 93 with sink on his fastball, and his quick arm and athletic frame promise more velocity to come. He'll show flashes of a quality 12-to-6 curveball at times, though it sometimes loses power and shape. He's working on a changeup and needs to create more velocity separation from his heater. Bradley's athleticism and clean delivery bode well for his future control. His stuff and command currently lack consistency, so he might spend two years in Rookie ball if he signs out of Redan. But his upside could make the youngest player on MLB Pipeline's Top 200 (he won't turn 18 until next March) worth the wait.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 40 | Power: 50 | Run: 60 | Arm: 55 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 A three-year starter at Loyola Marymount, Decolati's strong showing in the Cape Cod League last summer had many excited to see what he'd do during his junior season. A product of the Las Vegas high school ranks, Decolati has a lot of potential weapons he'll bring to the pro game. The right-handed hitter has a ton of bat speed and is capable of making very loud contact. He has outstanding raw power, but his aggressive approach has led to swing-and-miss issues that have hurt his performance this spring, which makes some wonder if he'll hit enough to reach that power consistently. Defensively, Decolati has a strong arm and will show the ability to make tough plays, but will boot routine ones at times. Primarily a shortstop in college, he might be better suited for third base, with some thinking a corner outfield spot would work. It's possible Decolati ends up filling a super-utilty role in the future. How much his bat can develop will determine his ultimate job and the team thinking they can help him tap into his offensive potential will be the one to take him on Day 2 of the Draft.

A left-handed hitter, Dunn has an advanced approach at the plate with very good plate discipline that allowed him to walk more than he has struck out over the course of his college career. The infielder reached double-digits in home runs as a junior, nearly doubling his total over his first two years combined, though his power at the next level is more likely to be of the extra-base, not over-the-fence, variety. With a below-average arm and fringy speed, Dunn is limited to second base. The Terrapins had a middle infielder taken in the fourth round of the 2017 Draft in Kevin Smith, now with the Blue Jays, though he’s a shortstop. Dunn may not go quite as early, but his success on the Cape, as well as his junior year, could get him off the board not long after.

Richan has missed a ton of bats this spring, while walking very few, thanks to a solid four-pitch mix. He’ll throw his fastball up to 94 mph consistently, complementing it with a pair of breaking balls. His slider will show flashes of being above-average and he’ll fold in a fringy curve as well. His changeup continues to develop and could eventually be average when all is said and done. While he has a high strikeout rate, he’s also been fairly hittable. Richan is more floor than ceiling, though he does have a solid delivery and a good 6-foot-3 pitcher’s frame. His upside is as a No. 4 or 5 starter, one who could come off the board in the top six rounds, which would make him the first San Diego pitcher to be taken that early since David Hill was a fourth-round pick of the Rockies in 2015.

Quezada isn’t the biggest guy in the world at 6-foot-1, but he has a fearless approach on the mound, going right after hitters with his three-pitch mix. His fastball sits comfortably, and consistently, in the 90-94 mph range. His changeup might be his best secondary pitch, though he also has a slider that should be a Major League average breaking ball in time. Quezada throws a ton of strikes with a free and easy delivery, and is at his best when he is commanding his fastball well. The right-hander has the stuff and command of it to potentially be a back-end starter at the big league level. He did look good out of the bullpen while pitching in the Cape Cod League last summer, where his aggressive approach could fit well.

That profile usually lands a high school pitcher in college, but he generated some late helium when he showed improved velocity late in the season. He still might not be easy to lure away from Clemson, where he could get a chance to contribute as a two-way player. Wrobleski's fastball jumped from 88-92 mph to 91-93 mph as the Draft neared, with his low-three-quarters arm slot creating angle and sink. His slider showed more power and flashes of becoming a solid second offering as well. His fading changeup could be equally as effective. Wrobleski shows a willingness to use all three of his pitches, though he sometimes struggles to control them. He has the athleticism and delivery to figure out how to locate his offerings and remain a starter for the long term. His development will require time and patience if he turns pro this summer, though he has a high ceiling as a lefty with three potential solid or better pitches.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 50 | Power: 40 | Run: 60 | Arm: 60 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Liniak missed most of his junior season with a broken hand, so while he did hit the summer showcase circuit, he was understandably rusty. The speedy outfielder has come back with a strong senior year in San Diego, adding some shine to what is a lackluster crop of SoCal talent this spring. There a lot of tools to like with Liniak, even if you have to dream on them a bit with this long and lanky high schooler. His bat has a ways to go, as he needs to add strength and some scouts would like to see him not as spread out in his setup as he cudrrently is. But he does have a frame to support good weight and there is bat speed and raw power to tap into. His best tool is his speed, which helps him on both sides of the ball. He’s even better once underway, which allows him to cover a ton of ground in the outfield. He has a strong arm to boot, one which would work from a corner, but he has the tools to stick in center field. Liniak is committed to stay at home and attend the University of San Diego, which could be tough to sign him away from. But his tools to go along with his performance this spring could entice a team to take a serious run at him in the top five or so rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 50 | Run: 40 | Arm: 50 | Field: 45 | Overall: 45 The son of seven-time Cy Young Award winner Roger Clemens, Kody is a better prospect than his brothers Koby and Kacy, both of whom entered pro ball as eighth-round picks. He played with Kacy in his first two years at Texas, spending most of 2016 at DH following offseason Tommy John surgery. Fully healthy again this spring, he won Big 12 Conference player of the year honors and led the league with 19 homers in the regular season after going deep just 10 times in 2016-17. A 35th-round pick by the Astros out of a Houston-area high school, Clemens' left-handed power and gritty makeup should get him selected about 30 rounds higher this time around. He has focused on getting stronger and pulling more pitches, managing to retain his control of the strike zone while increasing his pop. He has the upside of a .260 hitter with 20 homers per season, though that comes with the caveat that his track record of production consists solely of 2018. Clemens' below-average speed limits his defensive range, though his instincts and work ethic are assets wherever he's stationed. He played third base as a Longhorns freshman and was erratic there and has lost a bit of arm strength since having his elbow reconstructed, so he's manning second base this spring. He's an adequate defender there and fits the offensive profile better than he does at the hot corner.

He won the Southeastern Conference's batting title (.408) and freshman of the year award in 2016 and has stayed at Mississippi State for four years despite getting drafted by the Yankees in the 30th round as a sophomore and by the Mets in the 32nd round last year. One of the best seniors in the 2019 Draft, he broke Eddy Furniss' SEC career hits record in April with his 353rd. The scouting report on Mangum has changed little during his college career. A switch-hitter, he has an extreme contact approach that results in a lot of opposite-field singles but few walks and little in the way of power. His best tool is his well above-average speed and he's doing a better job of translating it into stolen bases as a senior. Mangum also has improved as a center fielder during his time with the Bulldogs, showing better reads and routes instead of just relying on his quickness to track down balls. He has a stronger arm than most at his position and touched 93 mph with his fastball when he started five games on the mound as a sophomore. One scout likened him to a faster version of Sam Fuld.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 50 | Slider: 55 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 55 | Overall: 45 After logging a 5.20 ERA in his first two seasons at Hofstra, Rooney ranked second in NCAA Division I this spring at 1.23 while also finishing first in hits per nine innings (4.8). The Colonial Athletic Association pitcher of the year, he set Hofstra records for ERA, consecutive innings without permitting an earned run (49 1/3) and strikeouts in a single season (108) and career (271). He matched Brian Verbitsky (Padres, 2013) as the highest pick in the program's history when the Dodgers took him in the third round and signed him for a slightly over-slot $563,240. Rooney succeeds more with command and angle than with pure stuff. His ability to locate his fastball on both sides of the plate and the plane his 6-foot-5 frame generates help it play better than its pedestrian 88-93 mph velocity. He also throws strikes with his solid low-80s slider and his fading changeup. Pitching in the Cape Cod League last summer helped Rooney realize he could compete against quality competition without overpowering stuff. He has been more aggressive about challenging hitters in 2018, showing no fear for pitching inside. He picked off 17 runners in 13 starts as a junior, and his ability to shut down the running game is another facet that gives him a high ceiling as a back-of-the-rotation starter.

Kelly moved from West Virginia to IMG Academy in Florida after his sophomore year of high school and quickly endeared himself to scouts, showing premium arm strength and performing well against top competition. The D-backs took him in the eighth round of the 2018 Draft, then went $350,000 above slot value to sign him away from a Louisiana State commitment. Arizona seldom assigns high school pitchers right to Class A, but Kelly debuted with Kane County and responded to the challenge by posting a 2.15 ERA and .189 opponents’ average, striking out 126 in 100 1/3 innings. With his prototypical pitcher’s body and a pair of plus offerings, Kelly already looks the part of a future big leaguer. In his first year in the system, he pitched in and out with a low- to mid-90s fastball that hitters struggled to square up due to its angle and late life. He has since seen that velocity tick up even more. His two-plane slider is a legitimate swing-and-miss offering, registering in the low- to mid-80s with hard bite, and he knows how to use it in concert with his heater. The organization sees potentially three dominant pitches and Kelly showed a willingness this past summer to mix in his split more which is a key if he wants to be a starting pitcher. Kelly made a big impression on the big league staff during Summer Camp and then carried that over to the alternate site. His fastball reached 98-99 mph at times. He is machine-like in his approach to taking care of his body and the D-backs rave about his work ethic. There are questions as to whether his future is as a starter or reliever. Whether he is able to master the split could go a long way towards determining that.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 55 | Power: 40 | Run: 45 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Playing for powerhouse American Heritage, alongside potential first rounder Triston Casas, Acton has gotten a lot of looks from a lot of scouts. Many like his offensive potential, but concerns about his defensive profile as a high school second baseman have limited his Draft stock. Acton isn’t overtly physical, but few doubt his ability to hit. After a bit of a slow start, he’s come on of late, showing a left-handed swing that should allow him to hit for plenty of average at the next level. There’s extra-base ability as well, though it might be more doubles than home runs. He is a solid defender at second with an average arm, but he doesn’t really profile well at other infield positions. And that’s where teams run into trouble trying to place him on a Draft board, as prepsters already at second aren’t typically high Draft picks. Acton is committed to the University of Florida and some see him re-emerging three years later after leading the nation in hitting with the Gators, kind of like a Jonathan India path with less power. It is possible a team will try to buy him out of that commitment in the top five or so rounds.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 Cole batted a mediocre .276/.350/.377 with five home runs during his first two seasons at Arkansas, then sat out fall practice with a stress fracture in his back. He has exceeded expectations this spring, hitting .333/.420/.559 during the regular season with a team-best 12 homers. His potential for average tools across the board and his strong makeup could land him in the first five rounds. A switch-hitter, Cole is equally adept from both sides of the plate. He has a history of making consistent contact and has gotten stronger, giving him the chance to hit 15-20 homers per year at the next level. He draws his share of walks and has average speed, not standing out in any particular area offensively but doing a little bit of everything. Cole is a little quicker once he gets going and scouts who like him think he might have a chance to play center field at the next level. He has manned right field for the Razorbacks, displaying average range, arm strength and throwing accuracy. He has the tools to at least fill in at all three outfield spots, enhancing his profile as a backup if he turns out to be more of a tweener than a regular.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 45 | Control: 50 | Overall: 45 Horace Greeley in Chappaqua, NY, has had just one player drafted from its baseball program, back in 2003. Neeck is sure to be the second as an intriguing high school lefty, though it remains to be seen whether he begins his pro career or heads to the University of Virginia. While Neeck isn’t the biggest guy in the world at 6-foot-1, there’s reason to believe there’s more in the tank as he physically matures because he’s athletic with a loose arm. He currently throws his fastball in the 90-93 mph range and has a good little slider that lefties really struggle with and that he successfully gets in under the hands of right-handed hitters. He doesn’t use his changeup much, which is a bit firm, but he does show some feel for it. He repeats his delivery, but he does wrap his arm behind his head, which causes inconsistent demand, something that should be correctable at the next level. It’s been a good spring to check out New York’s Section 1 high school baseball action this spring. Lenny Torres Jr. is likely to go ahead of Neeck, but the southpaw may not be behind by all that much.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 45 | Run: 50 | Arm: 50 | Field: 50 | Overall: 45 An all-state quarterback as a Pennsylvania high schooler, Datres has been a three-year starter for North Carolina at third base and has steadily improved his numbers each season. Draft-eligible as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2017, he went unpicked because of signability concerns. This year, he's arguably the best college third baseman available after lock first-rounders Alec Bohm (Wichita State) and Jonathan India (Florida) and could land in the first five rounds. Datres has gotten in better shape this season, adding strength and bat speed. He shows solid raw power in batting practice but it hasn't translated that way in game action, where most of his pop comes in the form of doubles. He makes consistent contact and draws a decent amount of walks, but he may need to get more aggressive and hit more home runs to fit the offensive profile at third base. Datres has average speed and moves well on the bases and at the hot corner. His arm and defensive ability earn average to solid grades from scouts, and some wonder if he might be able to handle second base. He may be more of a utilityman than an everyday third baseman if he doesn't do more at the plate.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Hit: 45 | Power: 40 | Run: 80 | Arm: 55 | Field: 55 | Overall: 45 Both of Marusak's parents were noted for their speed as college athletes at Texas Tech, where father Dean was a cornerback on the football team and mother Cyd ran the hurdles on the track team. Max could have a similar future because he's the fastest player on MLB Pipeline's Top 200 Prospects list and considered difficult to sign away from a commitment to the Red Raiders. He's tooled up, but questions about his bat may drop him low enough in the Draft to steer him to Lubbock. Marusak's explosive speed draws top-of-the-scale grades and can change games. He can turn routine groundballs into infield hits, creates havoc on the bases and chase down balls from gap to gap in center field. He also has solid bat speed and arm strength and at least average raw power. While Marusak can do more damage at the plate than a typical speedster, the question is whether he will. He has an aggressive approach, his right-handed swing gets too long and he'll chase pitches well out of the strike zone. A former shortstop who's new to the outfield, he also needs more polish defensively but has the quickness to outrun his mistakes.

bio_text: Scouting grades: Fastball: 55 | Curveball: 50 | Slider: 50 | Changeup: 50 | Control: 45 | Overall: 45 There are college pitchers who are labeled as “performers,” those whose numbers are better than their pure stuff would indicate they’re capable of. Then there are hurlers whose stuff is actually better than the stats they put up. Flynn, who served as Arizona’s Saturday starter in 2018, fits into the second category. Flynn has four pitches, all of which he is capable of throwing for strikes. He’ll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and he’ll back it up with a pair of breaking balls. He’ll throw a curve 79-82 mph and will also mix in a mid-80s slider that has cutter-like action to it. His 83-85 mph changeup gives him a fourth at least Major League average offering. While his command hasn’t been pinpoint, he is generally around the strike zone. Flynn’s ceiling is that of a No. 4 or 5 starter at the next level, though he did put up better numbers largely as a reliever as a sophomore. For him to go in the top five or so rounds, teams will have to look past his numbers and have a feel that his stuff will play in a professional rotation.

After pitching sparingly in his first two years with the Bulldogs, he created first-round buzz by showcasing perhaps better stuff than any college pitcher anywhere last fall. But he pitched himself out of Mississippi State's rotation a month into the 2021 season, barely saw action afterward and was left off the College World Series roster of the eventual national champions. During fall practice, Cerantola pushed his electric fastball to 98 mph and his curveball up to 87 with an astounding 3300 rpm. He averaged 95 mph and hit 100 with his heater this spring, but he struggled to throw it for strikes and it got hit when he dialed it back to find the zone. His curve remained devastating if not quite as powerful. Though Cerantola doesn't use his third pitch much, he does show some feel for a low-80s changeup with fade. But he can't succeed in the rotation if he can't dramatically improve his control and command, and the effort and stiffness in his delivery make it difficult to do so. He has frontline starter upside but comes with a lot of reliever risk and Mississippi State didn't trust him in high-leverage situations.

But an inconsistent prep senior season and worries about his mechanics rendered him unsignable, so he headed to North Carolina after turning down the Red Sox as a 38th-rounder in the 2016 Draft. A similar scenario is unfolding this year, when Berger has followed a banner summer in the Cape Cod League with an up-and-down spring and may not get picked high enough as a Draft-eligible sophomore to turn pro. Bergner can show flashes of three plus pitches but doesn't produce that kind of stuff on a regular basis. He often worked with a mid-90s fastball on the Cape but has sat in the low 90s this spring and his heater is hittable because it lacks much life. His best secondary offering is a mid-80s changeup with fade, though he lacks feel to spin and doesn't trust his curveball. The biggest issue with Bergner is his delivery, which is long in back and short in front. It affects the quality and command of his pitches and also allows hitters to get a good look at them. The hope is that he can clean things up and maybe become a mid-rotation starter, but the consensus is that he'll be a reliever who will have to work heavily off his fastball.

German, who began the year as the Ospreys' Tuesday starter but worked his way to being their Friday night ace en route to being a Golden Spikes Award semifinalist, has the chance to become the first. German has a solid three-pitch mix that points to a future as a starting pitcher at the next level. He'll throw his fastball in the 90-94 mph range and maintains his velocity, able to reach back for that 94 late in starts when he needs it. His breaking ball is close to a 12-to-6 curve with late and sharp break to it and he throws an effective mid-80s circle change that has the bottom fall out of it. He commands all three pitches well and has thrown a lot more strikes, while missing more bats, this year compared to his sophomore season. German has a limited ceiling, that of a No. 4 or 5 starter. But his performance in his Draft season has had more than GSA voters take notice, giving him a good chance to become the first North Florida pitcher to go in the top six rounds since the Tigers took Tyler Stohr in 2008.

He contributed to Coastal Carolina's 2016 College World Series championship as a freshman and unquestionably has a first-round arm. Yet he has battled the strike zone throughout three years with the Chanticleers and two summers in the Cape Cod League, making it unclear how high he'll get picked this June. Bilous has one of the best pure fastballs among college starters, sitting at 92-95 mph and topping out at 97 with sink. In shorter stints on the Cape last summer, he reached 99. His slider combines mid-80s power and late bite, serving as a wipeout pitch at its best, and he can flash a plus changeup with fade as well. Bilous is athletic but has a long arm action in the back of his delivery that hampers him from repeating his release point and keeping his mechanics in sync. He has averaged at least seven walks per nine innings in each of his three college seasons and may never have more than fringy control. He's probably best suited for the bullpen and has the stuff to handle a high-leverage role if he can find the plate.

The White Sox took a flier on him in the 36th round that year, knowing he was certain to honor his strong commitment to the University of Miami. He quickly showed his bat would play when he posted a .995 OPS as a freshman. He upped that to 1.025 over his first 16 games in 2020 and while his offensive production was inconsistent this spring, he was still thought of as one of the top position players in the 2021 Draft class. There is a lot to like about Del Castillo’s offensive profile, starting with his outstanding left-handed swing. He has a strong tendency to barrel up the baseball with an advanced approach, leading to more walks than strikeouts over his first two years with the Hurricanes. He hit 14 homers in just under 350 plate appearances at Miami. While Del Castillo didn’t open 2021 with a ton of pop and he didn’t dominate as much with wood during his time in the Cape Cod League in 2019, he did hit five balls over the fence in 37 games that summer. Just like when he was in high school, there are still some reservations about whether he can stick behind the plate long-term. His arm strength has improved and he tends to be accurate, but he’s not quiet enough with his receiving, showing a tendency to snap at balls too frequently. A team that feels he can improve and stick at the premium position will consider him in the top third of the first round, but his offensive profile alone will make him a first-rounder regardless of his defensive home.

Instead, he tore the ACL in his right knee playing pickup basketball and missed the entire season as the Wolverines came within one victory of a national title. He has been Michigan's best pitcher since returning and led the Big Ten Conference with 110 strikeouts in 81 2/3 innings this spring, though his stuff wasn't as sharp in 2021 after he used his downtime last year to add 20 pounds. When Hajjar is at his best, he works in the low 90s and tops out at 95 mph with his fastball, which has sinking action and gets on hitters quickly because of the extension he gets with his 6-foot-5 frame. He has sat at 88-91 mph with less life on his heater for much of this season. His best pitch often is his low-80s changeup with tumble, which he sells with fastball arm speed, while his curveball can be solid but has spent most of the spring as a loopy mid-70s offering. Though Hajjar has gotten stronger, he still has some projection remaining. While scouts hoped to see better stuff from him in his Draft year, he does have the makings of three solid or better pitches. He has done a nice job of tightening up his deceptive delivery since arriving in Ann Arbor, though he still can get more consistent with his control and command.

His secondary stuff is behind his fastball, though his slurvy breaking ball and his changeup show glimpses of being solid offerings. Some scouts don’t love his arm action and delivery, but with his athleticism, there’s hope things could be corrected with instruction. There are teams that don’t shy away from pitching projects, and Ras certainly would be one. At 6 feet and 170 pounds, Maldonado lacks projection and has a smaller build than desired for a starter. He looked like a top-three-rounds pick early in the spring, but his curveball regressed as the Draft drew closer, which may knock him down a bit. Although he's committed to UNC Wilmington, he's considered fairly signable for a mid-rounds prepster. Jarvis' fastball has parked in the low 90s all spring, and he should add more velocity once he adds muscle to his skinny 6-foot-3 frame. He works from an overhand slot that creates downhill plane but not much life on his four-seamer. He has flashed a solid curveball in the past but it devolved into a mid-70s slurve this spring. Jarvis has deceptive arm speed and fade with a changeup that may have more upside than his breaking ball. He has a quick arm but also a deep plunge in the back of his delivery that affects the consistency and command of his pitches. He'll continue to develop as a starter whether he turns pro this summer or attends college, though he might deal in the mid-90s as a reliever once he gets stronger.
